meta.blurb: Hana walked fast for a living, and now that she has retired she still cannot slow down. Then she meets Samir, who strolls the river path at a snail's pace. Beside him she learns to breathe as if each breath were new.
meta.bible:
Hana Kovacs: a retired postwoman of sixty-four, used to walking fast along her Round every day. Samir: her quiet neighbour, a retired carpenter who walks very slowly along the river path each morning. Mei: Hana's granddaughter, about seven, curious and playful. Hana's sister Edith: they quarrelled and have not spoken for a year. Mrs Okoro: a neighbour who joins the walks with her small dog, Biscuit. Teo: a teenage boy who joins with his headphones around his neck. The story takes place in one small town beside a River, with a Path along the water, a Bench, a Bridge and a hill with a view, over about one year from spring to the next spring. Key terms: Breath, Diaphragm, Belly breathing, Walking, Rhythm, Senses, Pilgrimage. Facts are hedged: at rest an adult breathes about twelve to twenty times a minute; slow breathing helps many people feel calmer, but studies differ and it is not a treatment. Traditions: Buddhist monasteries alternate sitting with slow walking; the Camino de Santiago in Spain is a pilgrim route, about eight hundred kilometres on the French Way; pilgrims at Mecca walk around the Kaaba; the labyrinth in Chartres Cathedral in France dates from about the year 1200. The words Spiritus in Latin, Ruach in Hebrew, Pneuma in Greek and Prana in Sanskrit are all linked to breath, wind or spirit. Voice and tone: slow, warm, concrete and a little humorous; one clear idea in each beat; nothing is forced and nothing is promised. Beat 200 reminds the reader that this book is general information and that anyone with breathing difficulties or who feels very low or anxious for a long time should speak to a doctor. Added for the full-length book: Judit: Hana's daughter, Mei's mother, a nurse who works long shifts. Bell Street: the first street of Hana's old Round.
Pip: Mei's small toy duck. Gertie: the name Mei gives to the grey heron by the river.
Mr Varga: an elderly man on Bell Street who lives alone and rarely gets letters.
More traditions, all hedged and treated with respect: Zen (Kinhin is the slow walk between periods of sitting); Aristotle in Athens and the Peripatetic school; Santiago de Compostela, the end of the Camino; Shikoku in Japan, with a pilgrimage of eighty-eight temples of about twelve hundred kilometres; the Hajj at Mecca, where pilgrims walk seven times round the Kaaba; Hindu and Buddhist walks round a sacred place, such as the kora round Mount Kailash in Tibet, about fifty kilometres.
Samir's grandfather was a farmer who gave Samir his wooden walking stick. Snail Club: the name Mei gives to the group that walks slowly each morning from the willows.
Teo is sixteen and has exams in the autumn. Mrs Okoro has trouble with her knee.
Edith is two years younger than Hana and lives two hours away by train. The sisters quarrelled a year ago, after their mother's death, about who had done more for her and about the sale of her small flat.
Laszlo: Hana's husband, who died four years ago, in November.
Leyla: Samir's daughter, who lives in a city about three hours away and has a new baby in late winter.
Mr Varga used to be a gardener. The librarian invites the club to lead a slow walk across the Bridge during the town's spring fair on a Sunday in April. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

beats.scene: Hana sits up in bed at dawn, an alarm clock silent beside her
beats.summary: On her first morning of retirement, Hana wakes before dawn with no letters to deliver.

beats.scene: Hana in an old coat strides along the river path, swinging her arms
beats.summary: Out of habit Hana walks fast along the river path, as if her bag were still heavy.

beats.scene: Hana passes a row of letterboxes on a street she knows by heart
beats.summary: Hana's feet take her along her old Round, past the houses where she delivered letters for forty years.

beats.scene: A neighbour waves from an upstairs window as Hana hurries past
beats.summary: Neighbours greet Hana cheerfully, and she realises that nobody expects her anywhere today.

beats.scene: A tall grey-bearded man walks very slowly beside the river in morning mist
beats.summary: Hana passes her neighbour Samir, who walks very slowly along the riverbank, and he nods to her.

beats.scene: Hana stands breathless on a stone bridge, looking at the empty river
beats.summary: Hana reaches the Bridge long before she needs to and has no idea what to do next.

beats.scene: Hana scrubs an already clean kitchen cupboard while the clock ticks
beats.summary: At home the kitchen feels too quiet, and Hana cleans a cupboard that is already clean.

beats.scene: Hana looks back over her shoulder at Samir, who crouches by a snail
beats.summary: Next morning Hana overtakes Samir again, wondering how anyone can bear to go so slowly.

beats.scene: Hana sits with the telephone in her lap and a cold cup of tea
beats.summary: Her daughter Judit telephones and tells her to rest, but Hana feels useless without work.

beats.scene: Hana lies awake while a street lamp casts a pale square on the ceiling
beats.summary: That night Hana lies awake, wondering what the quiet man at the river knows that she does not.

beats.scene: Hana walks beside Samir with folded arms and a frown
beats.summary: On the third morning Hana joins Samir, who asks why she is hurrying when she is going nowhere.

beats.scene: Two old tin cups of tea steam on a wooden bench by the river
beats.summary: Samir shares tea from his flask on the Bench and mentions that he was a carpenter for many years.

beats.scene: A carpenter's hands rest on a wooden walking stick beside a plank
beats.summary: Samir says carpentry taught him patience, because wood cannot be rushed, and that walking slowly is his way of seeing what he missed.

beats.scene: One boot print in soft mud beside a puddle under a willow
beats.summary: Samir explains that walking can be about arriving at each step, not about getting somewhere.

beats.scene: Hana counts her chores on her fingers beside a smiling Samir
beats.summary: Hana protests that she has things to do, but when Samir asks what they are, she cannot name anything urgent.

beats.scene: Hana and Samir shake hands in the early sun on the path
beats.summary: Samir invites Hana to try just ten slow minutes the next day, with no promises.

beats.scene: Hana walks alone on the path, glaring at a watch on her wrist
beats.summary: Alone the next morning, Hana tries to walk slowly and finds that ten minutes feels like an hour.

beats.scene: Samir and Hana walk slowly beneath new green leaves on the willows
beats.summary: Samir finds her at the willows, tells her that slow is a speed she can choose, and they walk together.

beats.scene: Hana lifts her shoulders high, then lets them drop, with Samir smiling
beats.summary: Samir notices that Hana's shoulders are raised and shows her how to let them drop.

beats.scene: Hana drinks tea at her kitchen table with the cupboards untouched
beats.summary: Samir asks if she will come again tomorrow, and Hana, surprised, finds that she looks forward to it.

beats.scene: Hana stands still on the path with her feet apart and eyes closed
beats.summary: Samir asks Hana to stand still and feel her feet on the ground.

beats.scene: A close view of two shoes on a path, weight shifting forward and back
beats.summary: Hana feels her weight move within her feet, from heel to toes and from side to side.

beats.scene: Two pairs of feet step slowly together on a path of fallen leaves
beats.summary: Samir shows Hana a rhythm: one slow step as she breathes in and another as she breathes out.

beats.scene: Hana's shopping list floats above her head like clouds as she walks
beats.summary: Hana's mind races with her to-do list, and she keeps bringing her attention back to her feet.

beats.scene: A small boat on the river tugs gently at its mooring rope
beats.summary: Samir tells Hana that the mind is not the enemy, because the practice is in coming back, not in having no thoughts.

beats.scene: A close view of a foot rolling from heel to toe on mossy stone
beats.summary: Hana feels the roll of each foot, from heel to toes, as she walks very slowly.

beats.scene: Hana walks from her kitchen to her hallway, counting steps on the tiles
beats.summary: At home Hana tries slow walking indoors, from the kitchen to the hall, and finds the short path enough.

beats.scene: Hana sits bored on the Bench, hands in her lap, under grey sky
beats.summary: On a dull grey day the slow walk feels boring, and Samir says boredom is normal and passes if she stays with it.

beats.scene: Hana stands tall, as if a thread were pulling gently up from her head
beats.summary: Samir shows Hana how to stand and walk upright, with the head lifted and the arms loose, which makes breathing easier.

beats.scene: A grey heron stands perfectly still in the shallows of the river
beats.summary: A heron stands still in the river, and Hana realises that she has walked the path for forty years without seeing it.

beats.scene: A hand rests on a chest beside a small clock on a bench
beats.summary: An adult at rest breathes about twelve to twenty times a minute, mostly without noticing.

beats.scene: A woman does a sum on a notepad on her knee beside a river
beats.summary: Hana does the sum and finds that she breathes more than seventeen thousand times a day.

beats.scene: Two people breathe out on a cold morning, small clouds in the air
beats.summary: Samir explains that the air contains oxygen, which the body uses, and that we breathe out carbon dioxide.

beats.scene: Samir draws an upside-down tree in the dust with his walking stick
beats.summary: Samir draws the airways in the dust like an upside-down tree, ending in tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood.

beats.scene: A dome-shaped muscle under two lungs, drawn in the dust
beats.summary: Samir explains that the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs, moves down as we breathe in.

beats.scene: A hand opens and closes a door in a gentle, steady rhythm
beats.summary: Breathing is unusual because it happens by itself but can also be guided on purpose.

beats.scene: A woman climbs a path uphill, breathing hard, with a sweating brow
beats.summary: Samir explains that a part of the brain sets the breathing pace by itself, and it speeds up when we climb or are frightened.

beats.scene: A woman rushes along a street, shoulders high, breathing shallowly
beats.summary: Hana notices that when she hurries or worries, her breath stays high and shallow in the chest.

beats.scene: Samir and Hana climb steps together, both breathing hard and smiling
beats.summary: Samir adds that fast breathing during effort is healthy, and that the aim is not always to breathe slowly.

beats.scene: Hana walks home at dusk with a hand on her heart, smiling
beats.summary: Hana walks home amazed that the most constant thing in her life is something she has hardly ever noticed.

beats.scene: Hana sits on the Bench with one hand on her belly, eyes shut
beats.summary: Hana tries belly breathing on the Bench, feeling her hand rise and fall.

beats.scene: A drawing of a lung, a dome muscle and a soft belly making room
beats.summary: Samir explains that the belly moves because the diaphragm pushes the organs aside, not because air goes into it.

beats.scene: A girl breathes in through her nose on a cold day, steam rising
beats.summary: Breathing in through the nose warms, moistens and filters the air.

beats.scene: A long ribbon unrolls slowly beside a short one on a table
beats.summary: Making the out-breath a little longer than the in-breath helps many people feel calmer.

beats.scene: Hana and Samir walk by the water, counting on their fingers
beats.summary: Samir teaches a simple count: breathe in for four steps and out for six, gently.

beats.scene: Samir holds up one hand on the path as a signal to stop
beats.summary: Samir's rule is never to force the breath, because comfort comes first.

beats.scene: Hana pauses with open hands at the end of a slow breath
beats.summary: Hana notices the small natural pause after an out-breath and learns not to hold it.

beats.scene: Hana lies in bed with a hand on her belly and a lamp dimmed
beats.summary: Hana tries slow breathing at night in bed, and her restless thoughts begin to quiet.

beats.scene: Hana leans on a tree, dizzy, while Samir holds her elbow gently
beats.summary: When Hana breathes too deeply and feels dizzy, Samir tells her to stop and breathe normally.

beats.scene: Samir shrugs beside a notebook of questions on the Bench
beats.summary: Samir says that slow breathing helps many people feel calmer, but studies differ and it is not a treatment.

beats.scene: Hana holds a single leaf up to the sun, seeing its tiny veins
beats.summary: Hana looks closely at a leaf and sees details she has never noticed.

beats.scene: Two people stand with eyes closed beside the flowing river, listening
beats.summary: They stand and listen to the river, the birds and the wind without naming them.

beats.scene: Hana bends to smell damp earth and wild garlic after a shower
beats.summary: Hana smells wet earth and wild garlic after the rain.

beats.scene: Hana holds out her open hands to feel the wind and sun
beats.summary: She feels the wind on her face and the warmth of the sun on her hands.

beats.scene: Hana presses her palm against the rough bark of an old willow
beats.summary: Hana touches the bark of the old willow and the cold smooth stones of the bridge.

beats.scene: Hana bites into a red apple on the Bench, juice on her fingers
beats.summary: Hana eats an apple slowly on the Bench and tastes it for the first time in years.

beats.scene: Hana lies back on the grass and gazes at white clouds
beats.summary: Hana lies back and watches the clouds, noticing the whole sky and its slow movement.

beats.scene: Five little icons for eye, ear, nose, hand and tongue on a bench
beats.summary: Samir suggests choosing one sense each day, to make walking richer.

beats.scene: Hana in a meadow with a plant guide, shutting the book
beats.summary: Hana starts naming every plant she sees, and Samir suggests simply looking without naming.

beats.scene: A woman sits quietly with her eyes open beside a calm river
beats.summary: Hana realises that the senses only work in the present, while worries and plans live elsewhere.

beats.scene: Hana smiles at her wandering thoughts like clouds over the river
beats.summary: When her mind wanders, Hana comes back without scolding herself.

beats.scene: Hana whispers a word as a cloud passes over the river
beats.summary: Samir suggests she quietly name her thoughts as planning, remembering or worrying, and then return.

beats.scene: Hana and Samir walk in grey rain under two old umbrellas
beats.summary: Walking slowly in the rain, Hana notices discomfort and finds that it changes.

beats.scene: Hana looks down at her wet shoes in a puddle, smiling
beats.summary: Hana's feet get wet, and she finds that looking closely at an ordinary discomfort makes it smaller.

beats.scene: Hana looks at her bare wrist where a watch usually sits
beats.summary: Hana leaves her watch at home and realises she has not checked the time for a week.

beats.scene: A quick runner passes Hana as she walks slowly along the bank
beats.summary: A runner passes them, and Samir says that slow does not mean lazy because the practice is about being present at any speed.

beats.scene: Hana frowns with arms crossed while Samir walks calmly at her side
beats.summary: On a bad-tempered day Hana is irritated by Samir's slowness, and he is not offended.

beats.scene: Samir sips tea on the Bench, a cup steaming in the cold
beats.summary: Samir admits that he often forgets to pay attention for days and that the practice is simply beginning again.

beats.scene: Hana counts steps on her fingers on the Path to the Bridge
beats.summary: Hana counts her steps to the Bridge on different days and finds the number changes with her mood.

beats.scene: Hana looks out of her kitchen window at a bright spring morning
beats.summary: After a month Hana notices small changes, though she cannot tell whether they come from the walks or from the spring.

beats.scene: Judit in a nurse's uniform hands Mei's small rucksack to Hana at a door
beats.summary: Judit, who works long shifts as a nurse, asks Hana to look after Mei, and Hana wonders how to keep a child busy slowly.

beats.scene: A small girl walks in slow motion beside Hana along the river
beats.summary: Hana's granddaughter Mei turns slow walking into a game, as slow as a snail.

beats.scene: Mei and Hana freeze mid-step with one foot raised, wobbling
beats.summary: Mei's snail rules are strict, and Hana finds that going really slowly is harder than she thought.

beats.scene: Hana crouches on the Path beside Mei, who points at an ant
beats.summary: Mei spots ants, a ladybird and a crack in the stone, and Hana crouches to see the Path from her height.

beats.scene: Mei blows a large soap bubble slowly on the Bench
beats.summary: Mei finds that a long, gentle breath makes a big soap bubble, while a hard puff makes none.

beats.scene: Mei lies on her back with a toy duck rising on her tummy
beats.summary: Mei lies on the grass with her toy duck on her belly and watches it rise and fall like a boat.

beats.scene: Mei points at the heron and names it, while Hana smiles
beats.summary: Mei insists that the heron needs a name and calls her Gertie.

beats.scene: Children play in a puddle by a school gate while adults hurry past
beats.summary: Samir says that children are good at being present, but that many people lose the habit as they grow up.

beats.scene: Hana kneels to hold Mei, who is crying after a fall on the Path
beats.summary: When Mei falls and cries, Hana breathes slowly with her, which helps a little though it is not magic.

beats.scene: Judit stands smiling at Hana's door, holding Mei's hand
beats.summary: Judit notices that her mother is calmer, and Mei asks to come to the river again every weekend.

beats.scene: Hana climbs a flight of steps, one hand lightly on the rail
beats.summary: Hana climbs stairs slowly, noticing each step, her legs and her breath.

beats.scene: Hana waits at a bus stop in the early light, breathing quietly
beats.summary: Waiting at the bus stop becomes a place to feel her feet and breathe.

beats.scene: A kettle boils on a stove while Hana stands calmly with her hands loose
beats.summary: Hana uses the two minutes of a boiling kettle to feel her feet and listen to the water.

beats.scene: A post office queue, with Hana letting a mother with a pram go first
beats.summary: In a long post office queue Hana breathes, watches the hurried faces around her, and lets a mother with a pram go ahead.

beats.scene: Hana sits in a clinic waiting room, hands calm on her knees
beats.summary: In a doctor's waiting room Hana practises noticing her breath instead of reading old magazines.

beats.scene: A customer fumbles with coins at a supermarket till while Hana waits
beats.summary: At a supermarket till Hana feels impatience rise in her chest, breathes, and lets it pass.

beats.scene: Hana walks slowly along Bell Street, looking up at the old houses
beats.summary: Walking her old Round slowly, Hana sees gardens, cats and carved doorways she never noticed in forty years.

beats.scene: Hana sits with old Mr Varga on his front step
beats.summary: Hana stops to chat with Mr Varga, who has had no letters for a year, and listens to him properly.

beats.scene: Hana pauses with a thoughtful look before answering a baker across the counter
beats.summary: Hana learns to take a breath before she answers, instead of finishing other people's sentences.

beats.scene: Three small marks on Hana's notebook page: door, phone and table
beats.summary: Samir suggests choosing a few everyday places for a slow breath, and Hana chooses the front door, the telephone and the kitchen table.

beats.scene: Hana climbs the library stairs with a notebook, past tall shelves
beats.summary: Hana wonders whether other people have found these ideas, and Samir, who says he is no scholar, suggests the library.

beats.scene: Monks in plain robes walk slowly in a line across a stone courtyard
beats.summary: In many Buddhist monasteries, monks alternate sitting meditation with slow walking meditation.

beats.scene: A bearded teacher strolls with students beneath the columns of a covered walkway
beats.summary: Hana reads that Aristotle's school in Athens was called Peripatetic, a word linked to walking about, and that stories say he taught while strolling.

beats.scene: Pilgrims with backpacks walk a long road between hills toward a distant town
beats.summary: Pilgrimage, such as the Camino de Santiago in Spain, uses a long walk as a spiritual journey.

beats.scene: A walker in a white jacket and straw hat beside a small temple
beats.summary: In Japan, a pilgrimage on the island of Shikoku visits eighty-eight temples and is about twelve hundred kilometres long.

beats.scene: A circular stone pattern on a cathedral floor with a walker inside
beats.summary: A labyrinth in Chartres Cathedral in France, from about 1200, invites a slow walking prayer.

beats.scene: Pilgrims in white walk in a great circle around a black cube
beats.summary: At Mecca, Muslim pilgrims walk seven times around the Kaaba, as part of the Hajj.

beats.scene: Walkers circle a mountain slope on a trail marked with prayer flags
beats.summary: Hindus and Buddhists walk around sacred places, such as the kora around Mount Kailash in Tibet, about fifty kilometres.

beats.scene: Four word cards on a table: spiritus, ruach, pneuma and prana
beats.summary: Many old words for spirit also mean breath or wind, in Latin, Hebrew, Greek and Sanskrit.

beats.scene: Hana and Samir sit on the Bench, a library book open between them
beats.summary: Samir says he does not claim that all these traditions say the same thing, and that Hana is not being asked to believe anything.

beats.scene: Hana packs a flask and apples into a rucksack in the dark kitchen
beats.summary: Samir proposes a dawn walk up the hill behind the town on the longest day, and Hana packs a flask.

beats.scene: Hana and Samir climb a grassy hill above the town at dawn
beats.summary: They climb the hill behind the town, one step and one breath at a time.

beats.scene: Two walkers rest on a flat rock halfway up, looking back at the town
beats.summary: Hana's breath comes hard on the steep part, and they rest on a rock, because breathing hard is normal and resting is no shame.

beats.scene: Samir holds an old wooden walking stick with a worn smooth handle
beats.summary: Samir tells Hana that the stick was his grandfather's, and that his grandfather taught him to walk slowly when he was a rushing young carpenter.

beats.scene: A young man planes a wooden board slowly in a sunlit workshop
beats.summary: Samir tells how, as a young man, he hurried a table and its leg wobbled, so his grandfather had him plane one board all day.

beats.scene: The town and river seen from a hilltop under a pale morning sky
beats.summary: From the top, Hana sees the whole river and town, and the view feels earned and calm.

beats.scene: The first rays of the sun rise over the hill and touch two faces
beats.summary: The sun rises, nothing dramatic happens, and Hana finds that this is exactly the point.

beats.scene: Hana looks down at the rooftops, her hand over her eyes
beats.summary: Hana wonders aloud whether her forty years on the Round were wasted, and Samir says she carried words between people.

beats.scene: Two walkers descend a steep path, with Hana stepping carefully
beats.summary: Going downhill takes as much attention as going up, and Hana breathes out as she steps down.

beats.scene: Hana naps in an armchair in afternoon sunlight, a blanket on her knees
beats.summary: Back home by seven, Hana feels pleasantly tired and sleeps all afternoon without guilt.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro and her small dog Biscuit meet Hana beside the willows
beats.summary: Word of the slow walks spreads along the street, and Mrs Okoro begins to join them with her small dog, Biscuit.

beats.scene: A teenage boy with headphones round his neck walks behind the group
beats.summary: A teenage boy called Teo comes too, with his headphones round his neck, because his mother asked him to.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro talks with wide gestures while the others listen with smiles
beats.summary: Mrs Okoro talks without stopping at first, and she finds the pauses hard until she learns to enjoy them.

beats.scene: Four people walk in silence along the river at dawn
beats.summary: Walking in silence together feels like company, and no one needs to talk.

beats.scene: Teo's thumb hovers over a phone in his pocket as he walks
beats.summary: Teo's thumb keeps reaching for his phone, and Samir does not scold him, but he tries ten minutes without it.

beats.scene: Biscuit sniffs a fence post with his nose pressed to the wood
beats.summary: Hana notices that Biscuit's walks are all about smell, and that a dog lives in a world of scent.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro sits on the Bench with a hospital letter in her hand
beats.summary: Mrs Okoro admits she is nervous about a hospital appointment, and the others stay with her while she breathes slowly.

beats.scene: Four people walk by the water at dusk with lights on the river
beats.summary: An evening walk beside the water, with swifts, bats and the first stars, feels peaceful.

beats.scene: Teo waits alone on the Bridge at dawn, hands in pockets, smiling
beats.summary: By the end of the month Teo is the first to arrive at the Bridge, and he says he likes that nobody asks him questions.

beats.scene: Mei draws a snail on a sign pinned to the willow trunk
beats.summary: Mei names the group the Snail Club, and the walkers agree that no one leads, no one is late and no one is early.

beats.scene: Two sisters in an old photograph stand arm in arm on a beach
beats.summary: Hana thinks about her younger sister Edith, with whom she quarrelled a year ago after their mother died.

beats.scene: A sealed envelope marked return to sender lies on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Hana remembers letters that could not be delivered and the silence between the sisters as a letter never opened.

beats.scene: A crumpled page and a pen on a kitchen table beside a mug
beats.summary: Hana tries to write a letter to Edith, and the three drafts are all angry or defensive.

beats.scene: Hana looks at a telephone on the table, her notebook open beside it
beats.summary: Hana decides to telephone rather than write, and she will take her slow breaths before the call.

beats.scene: Samir and Hana sit in the sun on the Bench, a cup between them
beats.summary: Samir says the aim is not to win or be forgiven, but to be present with whatever happens.

beats.scene: Hana's finger rests above the keys of the old telephone
beats.summary: On a quiet afternoon Hana sits at the table and takes a slow breath before she dials.

beats.scene: Hana listens with the telephone at her ear and a tear on her cheek
beats.summary: Hana and Edith talk, and the call is hard but kind, though it is not magic.

beats.scene: Hana presses a hand to her mouth, listening, tears on her cheek
beats.summary: Edith says she felt alone after their mother died, and Hana hears this for the first time.

beats.scene: Hana writes a date in her diary, with a small flower beside it
beats.summary: The sisters end the call without having solved everything, and agree to speak again on Sunday.

beats.scene: Hana and Samir sit side by side by the river, silent and calm
beats.summary: Afterwards Hana walks to the river, shaky and tired, and Samir sits beside her without a word.

beats.scene: Hana waters pot plants slowly on her balcony, with sunlight behind her
beats.summary: Hana does an ordinary chore slowly, watering her plants, with full attention.

beats.scene: Hana folds a warm towel from the washing basket, smiling
beats.summary: Folding the laundry, Hana feels the warmth of the towels and finds the repeated movement soothing.

beats.scene: Hana chops an onion slowly on a board, steam rising from a pot
beats.summary: Hana makes soup slowly, noticing the knife, the smell of the onion and the steam.

beats.scene: Hand tools hang on a wall in a sawdust-scented wooden workshop
beats.summary: Samir invites the group to see his workshop, which smells of sawdust and has every tool in its place.

beats.scene: Samir shows Teo how to sand a wooden box lid by hand
beats.summary: Samir shows Teo how to sand a small box by hand, and Teo works for an hour without touching his phone.

beats.scene: Samir and Teo rake red and gold leaves into a pile in the yard
beats.summary: Raking leaves in the yard, Hana feels the rhythm of the rake and the colours of the autumn.

beats.scene: Hana holds a bleeding finger above a kitchen knife and onion
beats.summary: One day Hana hurries a task and cuts her finger, and she learns that haste has a price.

beats.scene: Hana writes a postcard to Mei at the table, tongue between her teeth
beats.summary: Hana writes a postcard to Mei by hand, slowly, choosing each word, as a postwoman who has delivered thousands.

beats.scene: Mrs Okoro and Hana knead dough together on a floured table
beats.summary: Mrs Okoro teaches Hana to knead bread dough, and Hana sees that yeast, like wood, cannot be hurried.

beats.scene: Hana looks at a short list with one task crossed out
beats.summary: Hana tries doing one thing at a time for a day and feels less scattered, though she does not get more done.

beats.scene: Hana looks at a photograph on a windowsill, sad but at ease
beats.summary: On a grey November day, the anniversary of her husband Laszlo's death, Hana feels very sad.

beats.scene: Hana walks beside the river with her hands in her pockets, head bowed
beats.summary: Hana walks with her grief instead of pushing it away, and Samir walks beside her without trying to fix it.

beats.scene: Hana presses a hand to her chest by the river, eyes closed
beats.summary: Hana feels the lump in her throat and the tightness in her chest, and breathes gently without trying to make them go.

beats.scene: Samir sits on the Bench, looking at the water, his stick beside him
beats.summary: Samir says that he has sat on that Bench with his own sadness many mornings, and that grief is not a problem to be solved.

beats.scene: Hana speaks to Judit on the telephone, a mug and a tissue beside her

beats.scene: Winter breath rising in clouds as the group walks along a frosty path

beats.scene: Thick white fog hides the Bridge while four figures walk close together

beats.scene: Frost crystals glitter on a leaf, and boots leave marks on the grass

beats.scene: Footprints in fresh snow lead back along the riverbank behind two walkers

beats.scene: Hana lies in bed with a blanket and tea, looking at the rain

beats.scene: Teo holds out a tiny wooden snail on his palm at Hana's door

beats.scene: Four people walk slowly up and down a workshop floor on a snowy day

beats.scene: Hana holds the telephone in the evening with a calendar on the wall

beats.scene: Hana makes up a bed in the spare room, pausing to smooth the sheet

beats.scene: Hana lies in bed at dawn, smiling, with the window open

beats.scene: Hana writes a second page of her list, with a small leaf
beats.summary: Her list goes on: use the senses, do one thing at a time, and when the mind wanders, come back without blame.

beats.summary: Gertie the heron lifts from the river on slow wings, and everyone watches in silence.

B1B2: Hana woke at five, just as she had for forty years, and lay listening to the silence. There were no letters to sort today, and nobody was waiting for her.
Hana put on her old coat and went out before she had decided where to go. Her feet took her along the river path at her usual brisk pace, as if a heavy bag still hung from her shoulder.
Without thinking, Hana turned into Bell Street, the first street of her old Round. She knew every gate, every dog and every letterbox, and she almost reached into her pocket for the post.
A few neighbours waved from their doors, and one of them asked whether she was on holiday. Hana laughed and said yes, although she had no idea what else to call it.
Beside the river, a tall man was walking so slowly that Hana almost bumped into him from behind. It was Samir, her quiet neighbour, who nodded to her kindly as she hurried past.
Hana reached the Bridge in ten minutes, far sooner than she needed to. She stood there with her hands on the cold stone, breathing hard, and could not think of a single reason to be anywhere else.
Back in her kitchen the clock seemed to tick much too loudly. Hana cleaned a cupboard that was already clean, then sorted the spoons by size, and it was still only nine o'clock.
On the second morning Hana passed Samir at the very same bend, and again he nodded. She wondered how a grown man could bear to move so slowly when the whole day was waiting.
Her daughter Judit telephoned that evening and told her gently to rest. Hana tried to explain that she did not know how, because rest had always been something that happened after work.
That night Hana lay awake, her thoughts running as fast as her feet had run that morning. She kept returning to Samir and his unhurried walk, and wondering what he knew that she did not.
On the third morning Hana slowed down and fell into step beside Samir, with her arms folded. He looked at her kindly and asked why she was in such a hurry when she was going nowhere.

Samir led her to the Bench by the willows and poured hot tea from a dented flask into two tin cups. He mentioned that he had been a carpenter for forty-five years, and that his hands still missed the work.
Samir said that wood had taught him to be patient, because it splits and spoils if you hurry it. Now that he was retired, he walked slowly in order to see all the things he had missed.
Samir pointed to a boot print in the soft mud and said that every step is a small arrival. We usually treat steps as the boring part, he said, and wait for the real arrival at the end.

Hana told Samir that she had a great many things to do, and he politely asked her what they were. She began to count them on her fingers and was embarrassed to find that she could name none that were urgent.
Samir did not try to persuade her of anything. He only suggested that she should try ten slow minutes the next morning, and promised that she could go back to her old speed afterwards.
The next morning Hana tried to walk slowly on her own, and it felt like wading through honey. Her legs wanted to run, and she looked at her watch so often that ten minutes seemed like an hour.

Samir found her at the willows, looking rather defeated, and said that there was no need to be perfect. Slow, he told her, is only a speed that you choose, and they walked together beneath the new green leaves.
Samir noticed that Hana's shoulders were almost touching her ears. He showed her how to lift them once and let them fall, and she sighed like someone setting down a heavy bag.
At the end of the walk Samir asked whether she would come again the next day. Hana said yes before she had time to think, and then went home and drank her tea without cleaning a single cupboard.
One morning Samir asked Hana to stop and stand still, with her feet a little apart. She closed her eyes, which felt silly, and tried to feel the ground under her shoes.
As she stood, Hana felt her weight move a little from her heels to her toes and back again. She had never noticed that a person who is standing still is actually always making tiny movements.
Samir showed Hana a simple rhythm, one slow step as she breathed in and another as she breathed out. For a short time her feet and her breath were walking together.
Within a minute Hana's mind was racing again, full of shopping lists, bills and things she had forgotten to say to people. Each time she noticed, she brought her attention gently back to her feet.
Hana apologised for her busy mind, but Samir only shrugged. A mind that thinks is not a mistake, he said, and the practice is not to stop thoughts but to keep coming back.
Walking very slowly, Hana discovered that every step has several parts. The heel touches first, the foot rolls forward, and the toes push off, which she had done millions of times without knowing.
At home Hana tried walking slowly from her kitchen to her front door, which was only eight steps. It made her laugh, but she found that even a short path can hold a whole minute of attention.
On a flat grey morning the slow walking felt dull, and Hana said so rather sulkily. Samir agreed that boredom is normal, and said that it often fades if you stay with it instead of running away.
Samir showed Hana how to stand tall, with her head lifted and her arms swinging loosely. When her back was straight and her chest was open, she found that breathing felt easier.
One morning Hana saw a grey heron standing perfectly still in the shallow water. She had walked along this river for years, and it had never occurred to her that such a bird might live there.
Samir told Hana that an adult at rest usually breathes about twelve to twenty times a minute. Then he asked her to count her own breaths for a minute, and she was surprised by the result.
Hana did the sum in her notebook, as a postwoman will. Even at the slowest rate, twelve breaths a minute comes to more than seventeen thousand breaths in a day.

Samir explained that about one fifth of the air around us is oxygen, which every part of the body needs. What we breathe out contains less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, a gas that the body makes as it works.

With his stick Samir drew an upside-down tree in the dust, with the windpipe as the trunk and the branches splitting again and again. At the tips, he said, are tiny air sacs, where oxygen passes into the blood.

Samir drew a curved line under the tree and called it the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle below the lungs. When we breathe in, he said, it moves downwards, which makes room for the lungs to fill with air.
Samir said that breathing is rather special, because it runs by itself but can be guided whenever you choose. Your heart beats without being told, and you cannot simply decide to slow it.

Samir explained that a part of the brain at the base of the skull sets the pace of breathing all by itself. It speeds up when we climb a hill, and also when we are frightened, because the body expects to need more energy.
Hana began to notice how she breathed during the day. When she hurried, or worried about something, her breath stayed high and shallow in her chest, and her shoulders crept up again.
Hana asked whether she should always breathe slowly, and Samir laughed and said certainly not. When you climb steps or run for a bus, fast breathing is healthy, and the body knows what it needs.
Hana walked home at dusk, thinking that the most constant thing in her life was something she had hardly ever noticed. Her breath had never left her side, not for one minute, in sixty-four years.
On the Bench, Samir asked Hana to put one hand on her belly and the other on her chest. She breathed in quietly and felt the lower hand rise, and then she felt it sink again as she breathed out.

Samir explained that air never goes into the belly, of course, because it only goes into the lungs. The belly rises because the diaphragm moves down and gently pushes the organs below it out of the way.
Samir told her that the nose is built for breathing in. It warms and moistens the air and catches some of the dust, which is why he usually breathed through his nose while walking.

Samir said that making the out-breath a little longer than the in-breath helps many people feel calmer. He did not know exactly why, but he said it matched what he had felt for himself on many mornings.
Samir taught her a simple count for walking, which was to breathe in gently for four steps and out gently for six. When she ran out of breath too soon, she simply made the numbers smaller.
Samir had one rule that he repeated often, which was never to force the breath. If the pattern made her feel anxious or uncomfortable, Hana was free to stop and simply breathe as she liked.
After a few days Hana noticed a tiny pause at the end of each out-breath, before the next one began. Samir said that it comes by itself, and that she should never hold it on purpose.
That night Hana lay in bed with one hand on her belly and let her breath slow down. She did not fall asleep at once, but her thoughts were quieter than usual, and she was not at all unhappy about it.
One morning Hana tried too hard and took very big, fast breaths, and soon she felt dizzy. Samir told her to stop at once and breathe in her ordinary way, because gentle is better than big.

Hana asked whether slow breathing really works, and Samir answered carefully. It helps many people feel calmer, he said, but studies differ, and it is a way of paying attention, not a treatment for any illness.
Samir picked up a fallen leaf and handed it to Hana without a word. She held it up to the sun, and saw a whole network of tiny veins that she had never noticed before.
One morning they stood still and simply listened to the river, the birds and the wind in the leaves. Samir said that it is enough to hear the sounds, without thinking about what they are.

It had rained during the night, and the Path smelled of wet earth and wild garlic. Hana stopped and breathed it in slowly, and was astonished that something so strong had been under her nose all along.
Hana held out her hands and felt the sun warming her palms. A light wind touched her face, and she noticed that it was cooler on one cheek than on the other.

Samir suggested that she touch the old willow, so Hana laid her palm against its bark. It was rough and deeply grooved and a little damp, and the stones of the Bridge, by contrast, were cold and smooth.

On the Bench Hana ate an apple very slowly, as Samir had suggested. She noticed the crunch, the sweetness and the sharp taste just under the skin, and she realised she usually ate while reading the news.
One warm afternoon Hana lay back on the grass beside the Path and watched the clouds. They moved so slowly that she could hardly see them move, yet when she looked away and back, the sky had changed.
Samir suggested that Hana should choose one sense for each day. On Monday she might look, on Tuesday she might listen, and by Sunday she would have noticed a great deal.
Hana bought a guide to wild plants and began to name every flower she saw. Samir smiled and suggested that she sometimes look without naming, because a name can end the looking too soon.
That evening Hana realised something simple, which was that her eyes, ears and hands only ever worked in the present. Her worries and plans lived somewhere else, in the past or in the future.
Hana often lost her place and began thinking about something else. She learned to smile at herself and begin again, without scolding, as a kind teacher would with a child.
Samir suggested a small trick for the wandering mind. When she noticed a thought, she could quietly say planning, remembering or worrying, and then return to her step.
One grey morning it began to rain, and Hana wanted to go home. Instead they walked on under two old umbrellas, and she noticed that the cold and wet feeling was always changing, not staying the same.

By the end of the walk Hana's shoes were soaked, but she did not mind as much as she had expected. Samir said that this works for small, ordinary discomforts, but that real pain should never be ignored.
One morning Hana forgot to put on her watch, and she was worried about it for about five minutes. A week later she realised that she had hardly looked for the time since.

A young runner passed them with a friendly wave, and Hana wondered aloud whether she was being lazy. Samir said that slow is not the same as lazy, since the practice is to be present at whatever speed you move.

On one tired morning Hana found that she was annoyed with everything, including Samir's slow pace. She said so, rather rudely, and Samir only nodded and said that irritation was allowed to walk with them.
Hana asked whether Samir ever forgot to practise, and he laughed. Of course he did, he said, sometimes for whole weeks, and the whole practice was simply to begin again, as often as necessary.
Hana began to count her steps from the willows to the Bridge. On a calm day it took six hundred and twelve, and on a rushed day only five hundred and ninety.

After a month of walking with Samir, Hana noticed small changes. She was sleeping a little better and hurrying a little less, though she could not be sure whether the walks or the spring were responsible.
Judit worked long shifts at the hospital, and one Saturday she asked her mother to look after Mei. Hana said yes at once, and then wondered how a slow woman could keep a seven-year-old busy.
When Hana explained that they would walk slowly, Mei at once turned it into a game. They were snails, she announced, and the snail who moved slowest would be the winner.
Mei's rules were strict, because a snail could not stop and could not fall over. Every step had to take at least ten seconds, which made Hana's leg shake with the effort.

At snail speed Mei noticed everything, from a line of ants to a ladybird on a blade of grass. There was even a crack in the Path shaped like a river, and Hana crouched to see the world from Mei's height.
On the Bench Mei blew soap bubbles from a little pot. She found that a hard puff made nothing at all, while a long, gentle breath made a big wobbling bubble that floated over the river.
Samir showed Mei an old trick, in which she lay on her back with her toy duck, Pip, on her tummy. She watched him rise and fall like a little boat as she breathed.
When the heron appeared again, standing still at the edge of the water, Mei decided that it needed a name. She called it Gertie, and she asked how a bird could stand still for so long.
Hana noticed that Mei never needed to be taught how to be present. Samir said that children often seem to know how, but that many of us lose the habit as we grow older and busier.

One afternoon Mei tripped and scraped her knee, and she began to cry. Hana held her and breathed slowly, and invited her to breathe along, which helped a little although it did not make the knee stop stinging.
When Judit came to collect Mei, she noticed that her mother was calmer than before. Mei told her all about the snails and Gertie, and then she asked to come again every weekend.
At the library Hana decided to take the stairs instead of the lift, and to climb them slowly. She felt each step, her legs working and her breath deepening, and was at the top before she knew it.
The bus was late, as it often was, and Hana stood at the stop and felt her feet on the pavement. Instead of sighing at the empty road, she simply breathed and watched the light change on the houses.
Waiting for the kettle used to make Hana restless, so she tried something new. She stood quietly, felt her feet on the floor and listened to the water as it grew louder and louder.
Hana found herself in a long queue at the post office, where she had once worked. She breathed slowly, watched the hurried faces around her, and let a mother with a pram go in front of her.
At the clinic for a routine check-up, Hana had a long wait. Instead of reading the old magazines she sat comfortably, noticed her breath and let the minutes pass without counting them.
At the supermarket the man ahead of her took a long time to find his coins. Hana felt impatience rise like heat in her chest, so she breathed out slowly and let it go by.

One morning Hana walked her old Round again, slowly this time, and saw things she had never noticed in forty years. There were carved doorways, hidden gardens and a ginger cat that watched her from every wall.

Outside number twelve, old Mr Varga was sitting on his step, and Hana stopped to say hello. He had received no letters for a year, he told her, and she sat down beside him and listened for a long time.
Hana had always finished other people's sentences for them, to save time. Now she tried taking one small breath before she answered, and she was amazed at how much more people told her.
Samir suggested that Hana choose a few ordinary moments for a slow breath, so that she would not need to remember. She chose three of them, the front door, the telephone and the kitchen table.
Hana asked Samir whether other people had ever found these ideas. He said that he was only a carpenter, but that she might find answers in the library, and she went the next day.
Hana read that in many Buddhist monasteries the monks alternate sitting meditation with slow walking meditation. In Japanese Zen the slow walk between periods of sitting is called kinhin.

In the library Hana also read about Aristotle, a Greek thinker who taught in Athens. His school was called Peripatetic, from a Greek word for walking about, and it is said that he liked to teach while strolling.

Hana read about the Camino de Santiago in Spain, where pilgrims have walked for centuries to the city of Santiago de Compostela. The most popular route, the French Way, is about eight hundred kilometres long.
On the Japanese island of Shikoku there is a famous pilgrimage to eighty-eight temples. The whole circuit is about twelve hundred kilometres, and many pilgrims wear white and carry a walking stick.

In Chartres Cathedral in France there is a labyrinth, laid in stone on the floor about the year 1200. It has only one winding path, with no dead ends, and visitors walk it slowly to the centre and back.
Hana learned that during the Hajj, Muslim pilgrims in Mecca walk seven times around the Kaaba. More than a million people make this pilgrimage each year, and the walk is a central part of it.
In Hindu and Buddhist traditions people often walk round a sacred place, such as a temple or a hill. Around Mount Kailash in Tibet the walk, called a kora, is about fifty kilometres long.
Hana found something curious about old words from many different places. The Latin spiritus, the Hebrew ruach, the Greek pneuma and the Sanskrit prana are all linked to breath, wind or spirit.
Hana told Samir everything she had read, and he listened with interest. He said that these traditions are not all the same and that nobody was asking her to believe anything.

As midsummer came near, Samir invited Hana to climb the hill behind the town and watch the sun rise on the longest day. She packed a flask and two apples the night before, feeling like a child on a school trip.
In the cool grey light, Hana and Samir began the long climb up the grassy hill. They went slowly, one step and one breath at a time, and she was careful not to rush ahead as she once would have done.

On the steepest part of the hill Hana's breath came hard, and her heart was thumping. They rested on a flat rock, and Samir reminded her that breathing hard on a climb is normal and that resting is no shame.
Samir showed her the worn handle of his walking stick, which had belonged to his grandfather. The old man had taught him to walk slowly when Samir was young, hurried and always late.
Samir told her how he once made a table in a great hurry, and one of its legs wobbled badly. His grandfather made him plane a single board all day, and he learned more from that than from any table.
At the top of the hill Hana could see the whole town and the river, shining like a silver thread. The view felt earned, and for a long time she was quiet.
The sun came up slowly over the far hills, turning the sky from grey to gold. Nothing dramatic happened, and Hana realised that this was exactly the point.

Looking at the roofs of her Round, Hana wondered aloud whether her forty years of hurrying had been wasted. Samir said that they had not, because she had carried words between people, and that was never a small thing.
Going down turned out to be harder than going up, because the stones were loose and Hana's knees complained. She breathed out slowly with each careful step, and the slow pace felt exactly right.
They were back in the town by seven, and its streets were just waking up. Hana went home pleasantly tired, and she slept for the whole afternoon without feeling the slightest guilt.

Word of the slow walks spread along the street, and one morning Mrs Okoro appeared by the willows with her small dog, Biscuit. Biscuit looked at the slow pace, and then at Mrs Okoro, as if he had been tricked.
A few days later a teenage boy called Teo joined them, with headphones hanging round his neck. He explained, without much enthusiasm, that he was only there because his mother had asked him to come.
At first Mrs Okoro talked without stopping, about her knee, her cousins and the price of fish. The pauses frightened her, she confessed, but after a week she began to enjoy them.
One morning nobody said a word, and nobody felt that they had to. The four of them walked in silence along the river, and it felt like a kind of company.
Teo kept feeling for his phone in his pocket, as if his thumb had a mind of its own. Samir did not scold him, but suggested ten minutes without it, and Teo, to his own surprise, managed twelve.
Hana noticed that Biscuit stopped to sniff every post and every tree along the Path. Mrs Okoro said that a dog lives mostly in a world of smell, and that she had never given it the time to enjoy it.

One morning Mrs Okoro told them that she had an appointment at the hospital about her knee, and that she was frightened. They sat with her on the Bench while she breathed slowly, and nobody told her to cheer up.
One warm evening they walked beside the water instead of in the morning. Swifts were flying overhead, a bat flickered out of the trees, and the first star came out above the Bridge.

By the end of the month Teo was, rather to his own amusement, the first one to arrive at the Bridge. He said that he liked it because nobody asked him questions, and nobody minded when he said nothing.
Mei visited one weekend and named the group the Snail Club, which made everyone laugh. The only rules, the members agreed, were that nobody leads, nobody is late and nobody is early.
With more time to think, Hana found herself thinking about her sister Edith. They had quarrelled a year ago, after their mother died, and neither of them had spoken a word since.

Hana remembered the letters that could not be delivered, which she used to send back marked return to sender. The silence between the two sisters was like that, she thought, a letter that nobody had opened.
Hana sat down to write a letter to Edith, and the first draft was angry. The second was defensive and the third was a long list of excuses, and she tore them all up and took a slow breath.
In the end Hana decided that a telephone call would be better than a letter, because a letter cannot listen. She promised herself that she would take her three slow breaths before she dialled.
Hana told Samir of her plan, and he listened without giving advice. He said only that the aim was not to win the quarrel or to be forgiven, but to be present with whatever happened.
One quiet afternoon, Hana sat at the kitchen table with the telephone in front of her. She took a long, slow breath, felt her feet on the floor and dialled the number she knew by heart.
Edith answered, and for five seconds neither of them could speak. Then they began to talk, awkwardly at first, and Hana felt heat rise in her chest and breathed it away.

Edith told her that she had felt very alone after their mother died, and that she had been angry because she was frightened. Hana had never heard this, and she listened without interrupting, one tear running down her cheek.
When the call ended, nothing had been solved, and both sisters knew it. They agreed to speak again on Sunday, and that small promise felt like a door held slightly open.
After the call Hana walked to the river, feeling shaky and a little hollow. Samir was on the Bench, and he made room for her without a word and poured her some tea.

One October morning Hana watered the plants on her balcony as slowly as she could. She watched the water darken the soil and noticed the glossy leaves, and the chore took ten minutes and felt like a holiday.
Folding the laundry used to be a job that Hana wanted to be over. Now she noticed the warmth of the towels, the clean smell and the simple movements of her hands, and she found them oddly soothing.
Hana decided to make soup and to do it slowly, from the first onion to the last stir. She listened to the knife on the board, smelled the onion warming in the pot and watched the steam curl upward.
One wet afternoon Samir invited the group to his workshop at the end of the street. It smelled of sawdust and oil, and every tool hung in its place on the wall like a word in a dictionary.

Samir gave Teo a small wooden box and a piece of sandpaper, and showed him how to rub with the grain. Teo worked in long, even strokes, breathing out with each one, and an hour passed without a glance at his phone.
In the yard behind the workshop Hana raked the fallen leaves into a great pile. The rake made a soft, steady sound, and the red and gold of the leaves seemed brighter than she had ever remembered.
One busy morning Hana forgot everything she had learned and chopped carrots in a great hurry. The knife slipped and cut her finger, which was not serious, but it reminded her that haste has a price.
Hana had delivered thousands of postcards in her life, but she had not written one in years. She wrote one to Mei, slowly, with her best handwriting, and drew a small snail in the corner.
Mrs Okoro invited Hana to her kitchen to learn how to make bread. They kneaded the dough in a steady rhythm and then had to wait for hours while it rose, which could not be hurried at all.
For one whole day Hana tried to do only one thing at a time. She did not get more done, but she felt less scattered, and she had read that switching tasks often causes mistakes.
In November came the anniversary of her husband Laszlo's death, four years before. The sky was grey, and Hana woke feeling as heavy as a wet coat.
Hana went out to the river and let the sadness walk beside her, instead of trying to push it away. Samir came and walked quietly with her, and he did not try to fix anything.
Hana noticed the tightness in her chest and the lump in her throat. She did not try to make them go away, but breathed gently and let them be, and the sadness came and went like a tide.
Later, on the Bench, Samir said quietly that he had sat there many mornings with his own sadness. Grief, he said, is not a problem to be solved, but a weight that love leaves behind.
That evening Hana told Judit how heavy the day had been. Judit listened kindly, and they agreed that if the sadness ever lasted or grew too heavy, Hana would talk to her doctor.
A cyclist whizzed past so close that Hana nearly fell. Anger flared in her chest, but she took one long breath and let the out-breath carry some of it away.
One night Hana woke at three in the morning, worrying about money. She counted her out-breaths until her mind slowed a little, and when sleep still did not come, she got up and made tea.
Samir showed Hana how to move her attention slowly through her body, from her feet to her head. She found that she held worry in her belly, anger in her jaw and fear in her clenched hands.
Mrs Okoro said that feelings are like weather, and Samir laughed and said that the picture was old but good. We cannot choose the weather, he said, but we can choose whether to carry an umbrella.

Mrs Okoro said that she was short of breath on the stairs, and that she wondered whether the walks might cure it. Samir told her kindly that breathing exercises are not a treatment, and that she should see a doctor.
When winter came, they could see their breath rising in little clouds in the cold air. Mei breathed out as slowly as she could, to make the longest cloud, and everyone had to try.
One morning thick fog covered the river, and the Bridge disappeared completely. The world shrank to a few metres, and the sounds of the water and the birds seemed clearer than ever.
On a frosty morning the grass crunched under their boots and every leaf was edged with glittering ice. The Path was slippery, so Samir pointed out that slow, careful steps were also the safest.
The first snow fell overnight, and the Path was white and silent. When Hana looked back, she saw a line of footprints behind them, a record of every step they had taken.
Samir said that in hard cold it helps to wrap a scarf loosely over the nose and mouth to warm the air. He added that anyone with chest or heart trouble should ask a doctor about cold weather walks.
In January Hana caught a heavy cold and had to stay in bed for a week. Her nose was blocked, her head ached, and for once she did not feel guilty about missing the walks.
While Hana was ill, the others walked without her. Judit brought soup, Mrs Okoro sent bread, and Teo left a tiny wooden snail, carved in Samir's workshop, on her doorstep.
When Hana was well enough to return to the Path, her legs felt weak and wobbly. She walked only half the usual distance, and for the first time she was truly grateful that the pace was slow.
On the Bench Hana sat for a long time with her shoes off, getting her breath back. Samir said that rest is part of the practice and that slow walking should never be pushed, like anything else.
On the iciest mornings the Path was too dangerous, so Samir opened his workshop. They walked slowly up and down between the benches, and afterwards they drank tea beside the stove.
Through the winter the sisters spoke every Sunday, and the silences grew shorter and the laughter grew longer. In February Edith asked whether she might come and stay for a weekend.
Hana made up the bed in the spare room, smoothing the sheet and plumping the pillows. She noticed that she was nervous, but this time she did not scrub a single cupboard.

The train was twenty minutes late, and Hana stood on the cold platform, breathing and feeling her feet. When Edith finally stepped out of the carriage, she looked smaller and older than Hana remembered.
Edith walked down the street so fast that Hana had to take double steps to keep up with her. Hana laughed out loud, because she recognised her own old speed in her sister's back.
Over soup at the kitchen table the sisters talked for hours. When an old hurt came back into the conversation, Hana took one slow breath and listened instead of interrupting.

Each sister said what she had needed in the year of their mother's death, and each said sorry for particular words. They both cried, and nothing was tidied up, but something that had been tight became looser.
The next morning Edith joined the Snail Club by the river, though she said that she thought the whole idea sounded rather silly. Hana did not argue, and Samir only handed her a cup of tea.

At first Edith found the slow pace maddening, but then she saw Gertie standing in the shallows. She stopped for a full minute and noticed for the first time how quick and shallow her own breathing was.
On the Bench the sisters talked about their mother, who used to hum quietly while she walked. They remembered the tune, or something close to it, and hummed it together beside the river.
On Sunday evening Edith took the train home, with no big speeches on either side. They promised to meet again in spring, and Hana stayed on the platform until the train was out of sight.
One morning Samir announced that he would stay with his daughter Leyla for a month, because she had just had a baby. He was delighted, but he looked a little worried about leaving the group.
On the first morning without Samir the group gathered beneath the willows and nobody knew what to do. Their rule said that nobody leads, but somehow Hana found herself at the front.
Hana protested that she was no teacher, because she had been practising for less than a year. Mrs Okoro said that nobody had asked her to teach, only to walk, and that was something she could do.
The walk went smoothly, and the river looked exactly as it always did. Hana realised that the practice did not belong to Samir or to anyone, and that the Path belonged to whoever walked on it.
Mrs Okoro asked why slow breathing seems to calm people, and Hana found that she did not know. She said honestly that scientists were still studying it, and she felt relieved to have said so.
A postcard arrived from Samir, with a photograph of a tiny hand holding his finger. On the back he had written only two words, walk slowly, and Hana read them standing on the doormat.
Before a school exam Teo came to the willows looking pale and nervous. They breathed in for four steps and out for six, and Hana said he should talk to his mother if the worry grew.
Hana invited old Mr Varga to join the walks, and one morning he appeared in his best coat. He was the slowest walker of them all, and the whole group slowed down to match him.

In late February the snowdrops pushed up through the cold ground beside the Path, and the willows showed their first buds. Hana felt the year coming round, and she realised she had been walking for almost a whole year.

Samir came back at the end of the month, thinner but delighted, with a new photograph. He told them that a newborn baby breathes much faster than an adult, and Hana said that he was still needed, for tea.

In March the librarian invited the Snail Club to lead a slow walk across the Bridge during the town's spring fair. Hana said that they were not experts, and the librarian said that was exactly why she had asked.
Everyone helped with the preparations, and Teo designed a poster while Mei drew a long line of snails across it. Mrs Okoro baked bread, and Mr Varga, who had been a gardener, mended a bench.
Hana was nervous, and she asked Samir what she should say to the crowd. He told her to say less than she wanted to, and she wrote three short sentences on a card.
On Sunday morning about sixty people gathered at the end of the Bridge, in the April sunshine. There were children, grandparents, a man in a suit, three teenagers and a good many dogs.

Hana read her three sentences from the card, and then she added something of her own. This was not a cure for anything, she said, and anyone with trouble breathing or a long low mood should see a doctor.
Sixty people walked across the Bridge at a snail's pace, and for ten minutes the only sounds were the river and a bell. A toddler laughed, and Hana felt as if the whole town was breathing together.

Afterwards a man in a tracksuit told Hana that he thought it was all nonsense, because he walked fast for his health. Hana said that fast walking was good too, and that there was no single right way to walk.
Teo's mother found Hana in the crowd and thanked her warmly, saying that her son seemed calmer. Teo rolled his eyes and said that he did not have to love it, he simply came.
Under the willows there was tea and fresh bread, and a woman asked Hana how to begin. Hana said that she could stand still and feel her feet for one minute, and that this was already the practice.

That evening Hana told Samir that she had been terribly nervous, and he admitted that he had been nervous too. They sat on the Bench until dusk, watching the river darken, and neither needed to speak.
A year after her first morning of retirement Hana woke at five, as she always did, and lay in bed listening to the birds. This time the early hour did not feel empty, but full of small sounds.
Hana walked along the river path at an easy pace, noticing the blossom and the water. When she reached the bend where Samir stood, she did not hurry past, but stopped and walked beside him.
Samir said that the Path was never really for getting anywhere. Hana laughed, and said that after a whole year of walking it she felt as though she had arrived everywhere.

On the Bench Hana opened her notebook and began a short list of what she had learned. Feel your feet on the ground, let your steps and breath go together, let the out-breath be gentle and never force anything.
On the second page she wrote that the senses live in the present, and that one thing at a time is best. When the mind wanders, she added, come back without blame, as often as needed.
On the last page Hana wrote that ordinary life is the best place to practise. The front door, the telephone, the kitchen table, the queue and the person in front of you are all good places to begin.

In the afternoon Edith came for her promised spring visit, with the same small blue suitcase. She walked from the station a little more slowly than before, and she said that this was entirely an accident.
Hana walked hand in hand with Mei beneath the blossom, and she was honest with herself. She still forgot to pay attention for whole days, she still had much to learn, and she began again each time.
Beside the Bridge, Gertie the heron stood in the shallows, as still as ever. Then she lifted off, with a slow beat of her great wings, and the whole Snail Club stopped and watched her go.
Walk slowly, breathe easily, notice what is around you and arrive again at every step. This book is not medical advice, so please see a doctor if you have trouble breathing.

Now that his workshop was closed, he walked in the same spirit, slowly and with his eyes open, in order to see everything that his busy years had hidden from him. Hana, who had never thought of walking as a skill at all, listened with her cup halfway to her mouth.

Samir pointed with his stick to a single boot print in the soft mud beside a puddle, and remarked that a walk is nothing but a long chain of small arrivals. Most of us, he said, treat the steps as the dull part that must be endured before the real arrival at the end, and so we spend our lives travelling and almost never arrive. Hana looked at the print and thought it was an oddly convincing argument for a puddle.

Hana protested that she was far too busy to wander about looking at puddles, and Samir asked her, with perfect politeness, what exactly she was busy with. She began to count her tasks on her fingers, the shopping, the cupboards, the drawer of old receipts, and before she reached the second hand she fell silent, because not one of them would suffer if it waited until Thursday. Samir said nothing at all, which was, as it happened, the most tactful thing that he could possibly have done.

Samir did not try to persuade her of anything, which is perhaps why she found herself listening. He simply suggested that she might try ten slow minutes the next morning, as an experiment and not a promise, and assured her that her old speed would be waiting for her afterwards, exactly where she had left it. Hana, who had never refused a fair challenge in her life, said that she would think about it, and they both knew what that meant.

The following morning Hana attempted to walk slowly on her own, and it was like wading through honey with her boots on the wrong feet. Her legs strained forward as if they belonged to a younger and more impatient woman, and she checked her watch so often that ten minutes stretched into something close to an hour. It was, she decided, the hardest work she had done in her entire career, and she had once delivered forty heavy catalogues in a snowstorm.

Samir found her beneath the willows, looking rather defeated, and said cheerfully that nobody was awarding marks for slowness. Slow, he told her, was only another speed, like a gear on a bicycle, and anyone who could walk fast could learn to choose a different pace when she wished. They walked together under the new green leaves, and for ten whole minutes Hana did not look at her watch once.

Samir noticed, as carpenters notice a crooked board, that Hana's shoulders were hovering almost level with her ears. He showed her how to lift them once, as high as they would go, and then let them fall, and she sighed aloud as though she had been holding a heavy bag for forty years. Her shoulders, she realised with some surprise, had been waiting for her permission since the day she started on the Round.

At the end of the walk Samir asked, with no particular emphasis, whether she might like to come again the next morning. Hana said yes before she had time to think of a reason to say no, and she was astonished by how much she meant it. Back in her kitchen she drank a whole cup of tea, sitting down, without cleaning a single cupboard, and the clock seemed to tick much more gently than before.

One morning Samir asked Hana to stop in the middle of the path and stand quite still, with her feet a little apart and her arms hanging loose. She closed her eyes, feeling extremely silly, and tried to notice the ground pressing back against the soles of her old shoes. It was a strange request for a woman who had spent four decades trying to be somewhere else.

As she stood there, Hana felt her weight drift gently from her heels towards her toes and then settle back, as though her body were a boat rocking at anchor. She had never noticed that a person who appears to be standing perfectly still is in fact making dozens of tiny adjustments every second. It was the first time in years that she had paid her own feet any attention, and she felt a little guilty about it.

Samir showed her a rhythm so simple that she doubted it could matter, which was one slow step as she breathed in and another as she breathed out. At first the two refused to cooperate, and she stumbled over her own feet like a puppet with tangled strings, but after a few minutes they began to move together. For a short while there was only the step, the breath and the soft crunch of last year's leaves.

Within a minute Hana's mind had bolted again, dragging behind it the shopping, the gas bill, a conversation from 1998 and the question of whether she had locked the back door. Each time she noticed that she had been carried away, she brought her attention back to her feet, and each time it felt slightly less like dragging a stubborn mule. Samir, who walked beside her without comment, seemed to know exactly what was happening.

Hana apologised for her restless mind, but Samir only shrugged and said that a mind which thinks is not a fault, any more than a river which flows. The practice, he told her, was never to stop the thoughts, which is impossible, but to notice that she had wandered and to come home again without fuss. Every return, he added, was a small success, and a person could make a hundred of them in a single walk.

Walking at last at a pace that allowed such discoveries, Hana found that a single step is made of several distinct movements. The heel touches first, the weight rolls along the outer edge of the foot, and finally the toes push off, a sequence she must have performed well over a hundred million times without once observing it. She felt like someone who had lived for sixty years beside a library without ever going in.

At home that evening Hana tried the same slow walk from her kitchen to her front door, a journey of eight steps that she had made ten thousand times at full speed. It made her laugh aloud, since she felt like a very solemn duck, but she discovered that even so short a path could hold a whole minute of attention if she let it. She turned round at the door and walked back, which was, she thought, the first time she had ever enjoyed a hallway.

On a flat grey morning the slow walking felt merely dull, and Hana announced this rather sulkily, in the tone of a customer demanding a refund. Samir agreed that boredom is perfectly normal and suggested that it is often only the mind's way of asking for more entertainment, which it will stop doing if it is not fed. She stayed with the dullness for several more minutes and noticed, as he had said she might, that it slowly turned into something quieter and less cross.

Samir showed her how to walk as if a thread were pulling gently upwards from the crown of her head, so that the neck is long, the chest is open and the arms swing loosely at the sides. Hana, who had spent forty years leaning forward under a bag, was amazed to find that her breath seemed to have more room in this position. It was not a question of standing rigidly, he warned her, but of being upright and soft at the same time.

One morning, as she walked at her new pace, Hana saw a grey heron standing perfectly motionless in the shallow water, watching the river with the patience of a monk. She had walked beside that water for forty years and had never once noticed that such a creature lived there, and the thought gave her a small cold thrill, like finding a room in her own house. Samir, who had known about the heron for months, simply smiled and let her have the moment to herself.

Sitting on the Bench, Samir told her that a healthy adult at rest breathes in and out about twelve to twenty times every minute. He asked her to count her own breaths while the church clock marked a minute, and Hana, who was quite sure she was a fast breather, found that she was entirely ordinary. It was an oddly comforting discovery, since she had expected to be an exception.

Hana did the sum in her notebook, as a postwoman will, multiplying the breaths by the minutes in an hour and then by the hours in a day. Even at the slowest rate in Samir's range, twelve a minute, she arrived at more than seventeen thousand breaths every day, and she looked at the number with real respect. It seemed incredible to her that she had never thanked anyone for such tireless work.

Samir explained, in the plain manner of a man who has explained things to apprentices, that about one fifth of the air around us is oxygen, which every cell in the body needs in order to release energy from food. The air we breathe out contains somewhat less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, a gas that the body produces as it works and must be rid of. Hana thought of the whole town breathing in and out around her, and the air seemed suddenly crowded with invisible traffic.

With the tip of his stick Samir drew an upside-down tree in the dust, the windpipe as its trunk and its branches dividing again and again until they were too fine to draw. At the end of every twig, he explained, sits a tiny air sac, and through its wall, far thinner than paper, oxygen slips into the blood. Hana studied the drawing and felt oddly proud of the tree growing inside her chest.

Beneath the upside-down tree Samir drew a curved line, which he called the diaphragm, a broad dome-shaped muscle that stretches across the bottom of the chest. When we breathe in, it flattens and moves downwards, making room for the lungs to fill, and when we breathe out it relaxes and rises again like a tide. Hana put her hand on her ribs and felt, faintly, the whole machinery of her body doing exactly as he described.

Breathing, Samir said, is a rather special case, because it runs by itself all day and all night and yet can be taken over at any moment, like a door that swings by itself but can also be held. The heart beats without asking our opinion, and so does the stomach, but only a very few functions of the body can be handed back and forth in this way. That, he suggested, is why breath has always seemed to people like a bridge between what happens to us and what we do.
