Samir explained that a small region at the base of the brain sets the pace of breathing without being asked, speeding it up when we climb a hill and slowing it again when we sit down to rest. It also responds to fear and excitement, preparing the body for effort that may or may not be needed, which is why a nervous person's breath so often comes high and quick. Hana remembered the last steep street on her Round, and the long gasping that had always accompanied it.

Over the next few days Hana began to observe her own breathing, rather as one studies a neighbour. When she hurried, or worried about something small, her breath stayed high and shallow in the upper chest, and her shoulders crept back towards her ears as if on strings. It was not a disaster, she thought, but it did seem a pity to rush through the day on so thin a breath.

Hana asked whether she was now supposed to breathe slowly at all times, and Samir laughed so loudly that a duck left the water. When we climb stairs or run for a bus, he said, fast breathing is exactly what the body needs, and the practice is not about controlling the breath but about being aware of it. Slow breathing is useful when we have no need to hurry and merely need to settle, which, in his experience, was most of the time.

Hana walked home at dusk with her mind quietly turning over what she had learned, and it came to her that the most constant companion of her whole life was something she had hardly ever noticed. Her breath had been with her at every funeral, every wedding, every steep street, every unopened letter, and it had not left her side for a single minute in sixty-four years. She decided, rather shyly, that it deserved at least a little of her attention in return.

On the Bench, Samir asked Hana to rest one hand on her belly and the other on her chest, and to breathe as she normally would. After a few minutes she noticed that the lower hand rose gently as she breathed in and sank as she breathed out, while the upper hand hardly moved at all. It felt like discovering that a room she had thought was locked had never actually been shut.

Air does not actually travel into the belly, Samir explained, since it goes only into the lungs, and the name belly breathing is just a convenient way of speaking. The belly moves because the diaphragm descends and nudges the organs beneath it forward, and so a soft, relaxed stomach is a sign that the diaphragm has room to work. Hana said she was relieved, having privately worried that she had been doing it wrong for sixty-four years.

The nose, Samir told her, is built for the job of breathing in, since it warms and moistens the air on its way to the lungs and traps some of the dust and pollen that drift along with it. He usually breathed through his nose when he walked, as long as he was not climbing hard, and found it helped him keep to a gentle pace. Hana tried it on the next straight stretch of the Path and was pleased by how quiet her breathing became.

Samir said that many people find it calming to let the out-breath last a little longer than the in-breath, as if a long ribbon were being unrolled slowly beside a short one. He admitted that he could not fully explain the reason, and that scientists are still studying how slow breathing affects the body, but it matched what he had noticed on a thousand mornings. Hana, who believed in evidence, nodded politely and decided to test it for herself.

Samir taught her a simple count to use while walking, which was to breathe in softly for four steps and out softly for six, with no pushing at either end. When she found herself running out of air too soon, he told her to make the numbers smaller, since these figures were only a guide and not an examination she could fail. Within a hundred metres she had stopped counting aloud and was simply following the rhythm like a song.

Samir had only one rule, and he repeated it often, in the same quiet tone: never force the breath. If a pattern ever made her feel uneasy or lightheaded, she was free to drop it at once and simply breathe in whatever way felt natural. Comfort, he said, is not an obstacle to the practice but the foundation on which it stands.

After a few days Hana noticed a tiny pause at the end of each out-breath, a still moment like the top of a swing before it falls back. Samir said that this pause comes naturally to many people when they are relaxed, and that it must never be held or stretched on purpose, because forcing it would defeat its entire gentleness. She found that she liked it very much, and liked it more when she left it alone.

That night Hana lay in bed with a hand on her belly and allowed her breath to lengthen, without counting and without any particular aim. She did not fall asleep at once, as a tidier story would have it, but the racing of her thoughts softened into something more like drifting, and she was content to lie there. Sleep arrived at some point while she was not looking, which is how it generally arrives.

One morning Hana, eager to do well, took very large, rapid breaths, and within a minute the Path seemed to tilt gently like the deck of a ship. Samir steadied her elbow and told her to stop and breathe in her ordinary way, explaining that a gentle breath is always better than a big one and that no one ever needed to be impressive. If the feeling ever came often, he added, she should speak to a doctor, since he himself was only a carpenter.

Hana asked, with a postwoman's directness, whether slow breathing really worked, and Samir took his time before he answered. Many people say that it helps them feel calmer, he said, and some studies agree, but the results differ from person to person and no one should pretend that it is a cure for anything. He thought of it, he added, as a way of paying attention, which was valuable in itself and needed no further promise.

Samir bent down, picked up a fallen leaf and handed it to Hana without a word, as a teacher hands a pupil a question. She held it up to the sun and saw a delicate network of veins branching and rebranching, rather like the airways he had drawn in the dust. She had walked past ten thousand leaves in her life, and this was the first she had truly seen.

One morning they stood quite still and listened, and Hana heard the river chuckling over its stones, the birds quarrelling in the willows and the wind moving through the leaves like a hand through hair. Samir said that it was enough simply to hear the sounds, without deciding what each of them was or whether it was pleasant. For a few moments she stopped being a listener at all and became a place where the sounds happened.

It had rained during the night, and the whole Path smelled of wet earth and wild garlic, a green, peppery smell that seemed to rise from the ground like steam. Hana stopped and breathed it in slowly, and she was astonished that something so powerful had been there every spring of her life while she hurried past it. A smell, she found, can bring back a whole childhood in a single second, and then leave it again as quickly as it came.

Hana held out her hands, palms upward, and felt the sun warming them like a pair of small hearths, while a light wind stroked her face from the left. She noticed that one cheek was cooler than the other, a difference she would never have detected at her old speed, and the discovery made her laugh. It seemed that the world had been touching her all this time, and she had been too busy to feel it.

Samir suggested that she place a hand on the trunk of the old willow, and Hana, feeling slightly foolish in front of a tree, laid her palm against the deeply grooved bark. It was rough and damp and surprisingly warm in the sun, and a few paces later the stones of the Bridge felt cold and perfectly smooth by contrast. She realised that after forty years of delivering letters she knew the feel of a thousand letterbox flaps and nothing of the bark of a tree.

On the Bench Hana ate an apple as slowly as she could manage, at Samir's suggestion, attending to the crunch of the first bite, the sweetness of the juice and the faint sharpness just beneath the skin. She realised that she usually ate while reading the news or standing at the sink, and that she could not remember tasting an apple for twenty years. It was only an apple, but it was a very good one, and she gave it the respect it deserved.

One warm afternoon Hana lay back on the grass beside the Path and looked up, something she had not done since she was about nine years old. The clouds moved so slowly that she could scarcely detect their motion, yet whenever she looked away and then back, the entire sky had been rearranged, as if by an unhurried and very patient painter. She was surprised to find that she could watch for twenty minutes without feeling the slightest need to do anything else.

Samir suggested that Hana choose one sense for each day, and give it a little more attention than usual. On Monday she might look for colours, on Tuesday she might listen for the farthest sound she could hear, and by Sunday she would have noticed more of the world than in the previous year. Hana wrote the plan in her notebook with the satisfaction of a woman who had at last been given a timetable.

Hana bought a guide to the wild plants of the region and began to identify every flower along the Path, naming each one with the brisk satisfaction of a woman ticking off an address. Samir smiled and suggested that she sometimes try looking without naming, since a name has a way of closing a door, and we tend to stop looking as soon as we have said what a thing is. She tried it on a small blue flower and found that it grew stranger, and more interesting, the longer she failed to call it anything.

That evening Hana realised something so simple that she was embarrassed it had taken her sixty-four years, which was that her eyes, ears and hands could only ever work in the present moment. Her worries lived elsewhere, in a past that had finished or a future that had not begun, and so each time she turned to a sense she came home to the present. She wrote it in her notebook, underlined it twice and then, being a practical woman, went out to make supper.

Time after time Hana found that she had drifted away from the Path into thoughts about her pension, her neighbours or the price of eggs. At first she scolded herself, but gradually she learned to smile, greet the thought as one greets a passing stranger and return to her feet and her breath without blame. It occurred to her that this gentleness was something she had never been taught to give to herself.

Samir offered a small trick for the wandering mind, which was to give each thought a quiet label as soon as she noticed it, such as planning, remembering or worrying, and then to return to her step. The label, he said, makes a little space between the thinker and the thought, and a thought that has been named is much less likely to pull you along behind it. Hana tried it for a whole morning and was embarrassed to learn that she was mostly planning.

One grey morning the rain began, and Hana's first impulse, which was a strong one, was to turn round and go home. Instead they walked on slowly beneath two old umbrellas, and she paid attention to the damp air on her face and the chill in her fingers, and found that the discomfort kept shifting, growing sharp, fading, and then almost disappearing. It was, she realised, much easier to bear a feeling that she watched than a feeling she fought.

By the end of the walk Hana's shoes were completely soaked, and yet she found that she minded far less than she had expected, since a wet foot, examined carefully, is only a cold and slightly squelching sensation. Samir cautioned her, however, that this applied only to small, ordinary discomforts, and that real pain is a message the body sends for a reason and should never be ignored. She was glad that he had said so, because she had already begun to feel rather heroic.

One morning Hana forgot her watch, and for the first five minutes she felt slightly undressed, as if she had left home without her shoes. The church clock was always audible from the Path, however, and by the end of the week she realised that she had hardly thought about the time at all, and that the hours seemed longer, and kinder, as a result. She left the watch in the kitchen drawer, next to the receipts, where it seemed quite content.

A young runner swept past them with a friendly wave, and Hana wondered aloud whether the two of them were simply being lazy. Samir replied that slow is not at all the same as lazy, because the practice is to be fully present at whatever speed one happens to be moving, and the runner might be just as present as they were. We walk slowly, he said, because it is easy to notice things that way, and for no better reason.

On one tired and bad-tempered morning Hana found that she was irritated by everything, including the birds, the weather and especially Samir's slow, deliberate pace. She said so, rather rudely, and he nodded as calmly as if she had remarked on the temperature, and said that irritation was welcome to walk with them as long as it did not insist on leading. By the Bridge she had begun to feel faintly ridiculous, which was a great improvement on feeling cross.

Hana asked whether Samir himself ever failed at all this, and he laughed so warmly that the tea slopped in his cup. He forgot constantly, he said, sometimes for entire weeks, striding through his days as thoughtlessly as anyone, and the whole practice, in his experience, was simply to notice and begin again, as often as necessary. Hana found that this made her feel enormously better, and rather more likely to continue.

With a postwoman's love of numbers, Hana began to count her steps from the willows to the Bridge, and she soon discovered that the total was never the same twice. On a calm day it took her six hundred and twelve steps and on a hurried one only five hundred and ninety, and she found that the number rose and fell with her mood as faithfully as a thermometer. She decided, with some pride, that it was the most useful measurement she had ever taken in her life.

After a month of mornings beside the river, Hana noticed some small changes, which she was careful not to exaggerate. She was sleeping a little better, hurrying a little less and finding it fractionally easier to sit still, although she could not honestly say whether the walks, the spring or simple retirement deserved the credit. Samir, when she raised the question, replied that it did not matter very much, and that the Path would be there either way.

Judit, who worked long night shifts as a nurse at the hospital, asked her mother one Friday whether she could look after Mei for the weekend. Hana said yes at once, with great delight, and then lay awake wondering how a woman who had only just learned to go slowly could possibly keep a seven-year-old entertained. She need not have worried, as it turned out, because Mei had her own ideas.

When Hana explained that they were going to walk slowly along the river, Mei seized the idea at once and turned it into a game. They were snails, she announced, with shells on their backs and all the time in the world, and the snail who moved the most slowly would be the winner. Hana, who had spent a month learning to go slowly, discovered that she was about to be beaten by a child of seven.

Mei's rules were strict, and she enforced them with a severity that Hana recognised from her own years of work. A snail could never stop, it could never fall over, and every step had to take at least ten seconds, which made Hana's leg shake as she balanced on one foot above the gravel. She found, to her surprise, that moving this slowly demanded much more attention than anything she had done all week.

At snail speed Mei noticed everything, as though she had been given a magnifying glass for her whole body, and she found a line of ants, a ladybird and a crack in the Path shaped like a river. Hana crouched down beside her, with a creak of both knees, to see the world from a height of about one metre. It was a different country from the one she walked through every day, and it was crowded.

On the Bench Mei produced a little pot of soap bubbles from her rucksack and began blowing them across the river. She quickly found that a hard puff made nothing at all, while a long, gentle breath produced a big, wobbling bubble that floated away with a rainbow sliding across its surface. Hana did not need Samir to explain the lesson, and Samir, who had come to join them, merely raised his cup in salute.

Samir showed Mei an old trick that he had learned long ago and had never once forgotten, because it was so simple. She lay on her back on the grass with her toy duck, Pip, balanced on her stomach, and watched him rise and fall like a small boat on a calm sea each time she breathed. Mei declared that Pip was getting seasick and demanded slower waves, and she produced them with astonishing success.

When the grey heron appeared again, standing motionless at the edge of the water, Mei decided that anyone who lived by the river must have a name, and she announced that this one was called Gertie. She asked how a bird could stand so still for so long without getting bored, and Samir replied that the heron was not waiting for anything to happen, which was the secret of her patience. Mei considered this very gravely, and then she tried it herself, successfully, for almost nine whole seconds.

Hana noticed that Mei had never needed to be taught how to pay attention to the moment, since she did it naturally, with her whole body and with no embarrassment at all. Samir observed that small children seem to know the trick instinctively, and that many of us lose it somewhere between school and the first job, but that it is never really lost and can be recovered. He did not claim that it was easy, only that it was possible, and that it was worth the trouble.

One afternoon Mei tripped on a root and scraped her knee, and the howl that followed startled every bird along the Path. Hana knelt, held her close and began to breathe slowly where Mei could feel it, inviting her to breathe along, and after a minute the sobs grew smaller and further apart. It did not make the knee stop stinging, as Hana was careful to acknowledge, but it did help Mei to feel that the pain was not the only thing in the world.

When Judit arrived to collect her daughter on Sunday evening, she noticed at once that her mother seemed calmer, and that she had not looked at the clock for a whole hour. Mei poured out a breathless account of snails, soap bubbles, a seasick duck and a heron called Gertie, and finished by asking whether she could come again every single weekend. Judit raised her eyebrows at Hana over Mei's head, and Hana, to her own surprise, found that she was smiling.

At the library Hana chose the stairs instead of the lift and climbed them like a very dignified tortoise, noticing the grip of each foot, the work of her thighs and the deepening of her breath. It was a short flight, little more than twenty steps, but it held more attention than the whole of her old shift. She reached the top feeling pleasantly warm and not in the least out of breath.

The bus was late, as it often was, and Hana, who in the old days would have paced the pavement and glared at the horizon, stood at the stop and felt the soles of her feet. Instead of sighing at the empty road she breathed quietly and watched the early light slide down the fronts of the houses, one window at a time. When the bus finally arrived she was almost sorry, and that surprised her more than anything.

Waiting for the kettle had always made Hana restless, and she habitually filled the two minutes by wiping the counter or opening the post. One morning she tried something new, which was to stand quite still, feel her feet on the floor and listen as the water began to murmur and then rumble towards its boil. Those two minutes, which she had always regarded as empty, turned out to be one of the best parts of the morning.

Hana found herself in a long queue at the post office, a place where she had once been on the other side of the counter and knew precisely how it felt to be stared at by impatient customers. She breathed slowly, watched the tight, hurried faces around her and was filled with a sudden fellow feeling, and she let a young mother with a pram go in front of her. It cost her about three minutes, and she felt, as she reached the counter, richer by at least an hour.

At the clinic for a routine check-up, Hana was told to expect a wait of forty minutes, and she settled into the plastic chair with an unfamiliar lack of resentment. Instead of working her way through the pile of old magazines she noticed her breath, the hum of the lights and the soft shuffle of other people's shoes, and let the time pass without watching it. When her name was called she was surprised to find that it had been a rest and not a delay.

At the supermarket the man in front of her searched for his coins with maddening thoroughness, and Hana felt impatience climb through her chest like heat through a radiator. She did not scold herself, and she did not pretend to feel nothing, but simply breathed out slowly, noticed the tightness and waited for it to loosen, which it did within a minute or so. The man found his coins, smiled apologetically at her and she smiled back, quite sincerely.

One morning Hana walked her old Round again, slowly this time and without a bag, and she saw a carved doorway above a gate, a garden bright with sweet peas and a ginger cat that watched her from every wall. She realised that for forty years she had known the numbers on the doors and not one of the houses behind them. It was a little like meeting an old colleague and discovering that you have never learned her name.

Outside number twelve old Mr Varga was sitting on his front step, and Hana, who in forty years had never paused for more than a greeting, stopped and asked how he was. He had received no letters for a year, he told her mildly, and then the whole story of his brother, his garden and his bad hip came out, and she sat beside him for an hour and simply listened. When she finally stood up he thanked her with such unaffected gratitude that she had to look away.

Hana had always been a quick talker who finished other people's sentences for them, believing that she was saving everybody's time, and on this point her daughter had often protested. Now she tried to take one small breath before she answered anyone at all, and she was amazed by how much more people told her when she did not leap in. The baker, in particular, who had spoken to her for thirty years, revealed that he had once wanted to be a singer.

Samir suggested that she choose a few ordinary moments in her day to take one slow breath, so that the practice would grow into her life instead of living only on the Path. After some thought Hana chose three, the moment before she walked out of her front door, the moment before she picked up the telephone and the moment before she sat down at the kitchen table. She wrote them in her notebook, where they looked rather small, and yet she suspected that they were going to matter.

Hana asked Samir whether other people, in other times and places, had ever discovered these simple ideas for themselves. He replied that he was only a carpenter and no kind of scholar, and that he would not like to speak for anyone else's tradition, but that the library might be able to tell her something. She went the very next morning with a new notebook, and she climbed the stairs slowly.

Among the first things Hana read was that in many Buddhist monasteries the monks alternate periods of sitting meditation with periods of very slow walking, as though the stillness of one were carried into the movement of the other. In Japanese Zen the walk between sittings is known as kinhin, and the monks pace around the hall in a line, hands held at the chest and eyes lowered. She read the passage twice, and then, as a test, tried it in her kitchen.

In the library Hana also read about Aristotle, the great Greek thinker, who taught in Athens more than two thousand years ago. His school was known as Peripatetic, a name connected to a Greek word for walking about, and it is said that he taught as he strolled. Hana liked the picture, although she noted that nobody could be certain how much of the story was true.

Hana read about the Camino de Santiago, the old pilgrim route across northern Spain, along which people have walked for many centuries towards the city of Santiago de Compostela. The most popular way, called the French Way, is about eight hundred kilometres long and usually takes around five weeks, and some walkers go for faith, some for adventure and some simply to be alone with their thoughts. She tried to imagine eight hundred kilometres, and then, with relief, she imagined the single step.

On the Japanese island of Shikoku there is a famous pilgrimage that visits eighty-eight temples, and the whole circuit is about twelve hundred kilometres long. Many of those who walk it wear white clothes and a straw hat and carry a staff, and they stop at each temple to pay their respects before moving on. Hana noticed that, like the Camino, it is made of the same unglamorous material as her own morning, namely one foot placed in front of the other.

In Chartres Cathedral in France there is a labyrinth set into the stone floor of the nave, which dates from about the year 1200 and which has been walked by visitors for centuries. Unlike a maze, it has a single winding path with no dead ends, so the walker has nothing to decide and can give the whole attention to the slow journey to the centre and back. For many it is a form of walking prayer, and Hana thought it a beautiful idea, whatever one believed.

Hana learned that during the Hajj, the great pilgrimage of Islam, Muslim pilgrims in Mecca walk seven times around the Kaaba, the sacred building at the centre of the Great Mosque. More than a million people make this journey each year, and the walk is one of the central acts of it, done in company and with a sense of devotion. She read the paragraph with the respect that is owed to something one has not experienced and does not pretend to understand.

In Hindu and Buddhist traditions, Hana read, it is common to walk in a slow circle around a sacred place, such as a temple, a shrine or even an entire hill, as a way of honouring it. Around Mount Kailash in Tibet the walk is called a kora and is about fifty kilometres long, and it is made by Hindus, Buddhists and others who hold the mountain holy. It struck her that human beings, in very different centuries and countries, have kept coming back to the same simple practice, which is to walk with attention.

Hana found something curious in the dictionary, which is that in several ancient languages the word for spirit is also a word for breath or wind, as in the Latin spiritus, the Hebrew ruach and the Greek pneuma. In Sanskrit the word prana is linked to breath and life energy, and peoples who were far apart in place and time seem to have noticed the same closeness. She wondered whether people have always felt, as she now did, that breath is something more than air.

Hana told Samir everything that she had read, and he listened with real interest, asking questions that showed how little he had known himself. He said that these traditions differ in their beliefs and their reasons, and that he would never claim they all said the same thing, only that many of them valued slow steps and an awareness of the breath. Nobody was asking her to believe anything, he added, and Hana, who had no particular faith, found that she could take this in without difficulty.

As midsummer came near, Samir invited Hana to climb the hill behind the town and watch the sun rise on the longest day of the year. She packed a flask of tea and two apples the night before, and she set her alarm for four, an hour at which she had often been awake but never glad about it. She felt like a child before a school trip, and she was not at all ashamed of it.

In the cool grey light of four thirty they began to climb the grassy hill above the town, and the path soon turned steep and stony. They went slowly, one step and one breath at a time, and Hana, who in her old life would have raced to the top and been disappointed by it, kept her pace to the rhythm of her breath. A thrush was already singing somewhere in the thorn bushes, as if it too were on a very early shift.

On the steepest stretch of the hill Hana's breath came hard and loud, and she could feel her heart thumping in her ears like a drum in a cellar. They rested on a flat rock, and Samir reminded her that breathing hard on a climb is entirely normal and that stopping is not failure, but only a way of arriving more comfortably. She waited for her breath to settle, which it did, much faster than it would have a month ago.

Samir held out his walking stick for her to see, the handle worn smooth and dark by a century of hands, and told her that it had belonged to his grandfather. The old man had been a farmer, and he had taught his grandson to walk slowly when Samir was a young carpenter, always rushing and always late for the next job. Hana ran her thumb along the polished wood and felt that she was touching a very long chain of patience.

Samir told her how, at twenty, he had once built a table in a tremendous hurry, and how one of its legs had wobbled so badly that the customer brought it back. His grandfather had said nothing at all, but had given him a single board and told him to plane it, and nothing else, until the day was over. It was the longest and most boring day of Samir's youth, he said, and it was the day he began to understand wood.

At the top of the hill the whole valley lay below them, the town in its bowl of roofs and the river looping through it like a silver thread dropped on a green cloth. Hana had never seen it all at once before, and the view felt earned in a way that no view from a car window could, since every step of it was in her legs. For a long time she said nothing, and Samir was kind enough to say nothing either.

The sun climbed slowly over the far hills, turning the grey sky first to pale yellow and then to gold, and the shadows of the two walkers stretched long across the grass. Nothing dramatic happened, no voice spoke and no revelation arrived, and Hana realised with some amusement that this was exactly the point. She simply sat and breathed and watched the light spread across the town, and that was, quite sufficiently, enough.

Looking down at the roofs of her old Round, Hana wondered aloud whether her forty years of hurrying had been a kind of waste, a long race to a finish line that did not exist. Samir answered gently that they had not been wasted at all, because she had carried news, bills, birthday cards and love letters to thousands of people, and that was never a small thing. He added that the hurry had been a part of the work, and that it was only now that the work was finished that she could let it go.

Going down turned out to be harder than going up, because the stones were loose, the slope was steep and Hana's knees complained at every jolt. She breathed out slowly with each careful step, as Samir did, and discovered that a slow descent asks for the same close attention as a climb, only with different muscles. Halfway down, she realised she was thoroughly enjoying herself, and the thought nearly made her miss her footing.

They were back in the town by seven, while the first buses rumbled past and the shutters of the baker's shop were rattling upwards. Hana went home pleasantly tired, as she had not been since her working years, and she slept in her armchair for the entire afternoon without feeling the least trace of guilt. It occurred to her, as she drifted off, that a day which began on a hill could never quite be a wasted one.

Word of the slow morning walks spread along the street, as news always does, and one July morning Mrs Okoro appeared beneath the willows with her small, impatient dog, Biscuit. The dog looked at the slow pace of the walkers, then at his owner, with an expression of visible betrayal, and sat down on the path to make his feelings known. Mrs Okoro, who was a cheerful woman and not easily embarrassed, said that he would learn.

A few days later a teenage boy called Teo slouched up to the willows with his headphones hanging round his neck and his hands deep in his pockets. He explained, with the weary honesty of the very young, that he was only there because his mother had asked him to come and that he did not expect to enjoy it. Samir said that this was an excellent reason, and that no other reason was needed.

At first Mrs Okoro talked without pausing for breath, about her knee, her cousins, the price of fish and the shocking state of the bus timetable. She confessed that silence frightened her slightly, since it left room for thoughts she did not wish to hear, but after about a week she began to enjoy the pauses, and even to fill them with a hum. Hana, who knew a great deal about talking quickly herself, felt a warm and slightly guilty fellow feeling.

One morning, without any plan, nobody said a word, and nobody felt that they had to, and the four of them walked on in silence beside the water. It was a different kind of silence from the one Hana remembered in her empty kitchen, since this one was shared and had company in it, like a room in which people are reading. Even Biscuit, trotting at the end of his lead, seemed to feel that something was being observed.

Teo's hand kept drifting towards the phone in his pocket, as though his thumb had a will of its own, and each time he caught it, he looked guilty and slightly alarmed. Samir did not scold him in the least, but merely suggested that he try ten minutes without it, and Teo, to his own surprise, managed twelve. He said afterwards that it was like putting down a heavy bag he had not known he was carrying.

Hana noticed that Biscuit stopped to investigate every fence post, every tree root and every suspicious tuft of grass, and that now, at a slow pace, nobody hurried him along. Mrs Okoro said that a dog lives largely in a world of scent, that she had spent years dragging him away from it and that she was now ashamed. Biscuit, who understood none of this, wagged his tail with the contentment of a creature at last allowed to read his newspaper.

One morning Mrs Okoro admitted, in a very small voice, that she had an appointment at the hospital next week about her knee and that she was more frightened than she wished to say. They sat with her on the Bench while she breathed slowly, and nobody told her not to worry or to cheer up, which Hana had come to see as the kindest response of all. The breathing did not take away her fear, but it gave the fear a little less room to stretch.

One warm evening, for a change, they walked beside the water at dusk instead of at dawn, and the town seemed to be exhaling after a long day. Swifts screamed overhead in their last circuits of the sky, a bat flickered out of the willows and the lights of the Bridge began to tremble in the river. Hana noticed that the evening had its own kind of stillness, softer than the morning's, like a hand laid gently on a shoulder.

By the end of the month Teo was, rather to his own amusement, the first one to arrive at the Bridge, where he stood leaning on the parapet with his headphones round his neck. He told Hana that he came because nobody asked him questions or minded when he said nothing, and that at school there were always people wanting something from him. He was sixteen, with exams in the autumn, and he did not say that the walks helped him, only that he would be there tomorrow.

When Mei visited that weekend she took one look at the little group beneath the willows and named it the Snail Club, and the name stuck at once, to everyone's delight. The members agreed, without a vote, upon three rules: that nobody would lead, that nobody would be late and that nobody would be early, since a snail does not recognise those words. Mei drew an official badge on a scrap of paper, a very small snail with a very large smile, and pinned it to the willow.

With so much more time to think, Hana found that her thoughts kept returning to her younger sister Edith, who lived two hours away by train. They had quarrelled a year ago, soon after their mother died, about who had done more for her and what should happen to her small flat, and neither of them had spoken a word to the other since. It was the one subject that had never been fast enough to run away from.

Hana remembered the letters that could never be delivered, which she had once stamped and sent back to their senders, and she thought that the silence between her and Edith was just such a letter. It had been written on both sides, addressed on both sides and returned from both sides, and it sat unopened in the middle of her life, gathering a faint dust. She did not know yet what she would do about it, only that she could no longer pretend that it was not there.

Hana sat down at the kitchen table to write Edith a letter, and the first draft came out angry, the second defensive and the third a long list of excuses that she tore up in shame. She sat with the pen in her hand and breathed, and slowly she noticed that her jaw was clenched and her shoulders had risen up to her ears. When she let them drop, the right words did not arrive, but the wrong ones seemed to lose some of their heat.

In the end Hana decided that a telephone call would be better than a letter, since a letter cannot hear what the other person says and a voice can be corrected as it goes. She promised herself that she would take her slow breath before dialling, as she had agreed with the notebook, and that she would try to listen more than she spoke. It was a modest plan, and it frightened her much more than any dog on her Round had ever done.

Hana told Samir about her plan, and he listened for a long time without offering any advice, which was how she knew he was a wise man. He said only that the aim was perhaps not to win the argument, or to be forgiven, or even to make things right, but to be as present as she could with whatever might happen. He added that he could not promise anything, and she was grateful that he did not.

One quiet October afternoon Hana sat down at the kitchen table, put the telephone in front of her and took one long, slow breath, feeling her feet on the cold tiles. Her finger hovered over the keys for a moment, as it had once hovered above the letterbox of a house with a very large dog, and then she dialled the number that she knew by heart. It rang four times, and every single ring seemed to last for roughly a week.

Edith answered on the fifth ring, and for several seconds neither of them could think of a single word, so that the line crackled quietly between them like a small fire. Then they began to talk, awkwardly and then less awkwardly, and several times Hana felt the old heat rising in her chest and simply breathed it away instead of answering sharply. It was not, strictly speaking, a pleasant conversation, but it was an honest one, and Hana was glad of it.

Edith told her, in a voice that shook slightly, that she had felt terribly alone after their mother died, and that her anger had really been fear wearing a different coat. Hana had never heard this before, and instead of defending herself she took a breath and listened, one tear running slowly down her cheek and into the corner of her mouth. She realised that in a year of rehearsing her own side she had never once imagined her sister's.

When the call finally ended, after almost an hour, nothing whatever had been solved, and both sisters knew it perfectly well. They agreed to speak again on Sunday, and that small promise felt to Hana like a door held slightly open on a landing that she had forgotten was there. She wrote the date in her diary and drew a tiny flower beside it, which she had not done since the age of eleven.

After the call Hana walked down to the river with her legs feeling oddly soft, and her heart seemed to have been taken out and put back a little to one side. Samir was sitting on the Bench, and he made room for her without a word and poured out a cup of tea, and for a long time they watched the water together. Eventually, to her own astonishment, Hana began to laugh, and a minute later she was crying, and neither seemed to be any trouble to him.

One October morning Hana watered the pot plants on her balcony as slowly as she could manage, pouring in small amounts and watching the dry soil darken and drink. She noticed the glossy leaves of the geranium, a spider's thread between two stalks and the weight of the can in her hand, and the chore, which had once taken a minute, took ten and felt rather like a holiday. It was the first time she had ever seen the plants as living things and not as a duty.

Folding the laundry had always been a job that Hana wished to be finished before it began, and she usually did it in front of the television with her mind somewhere else entirely. Now she noticed the warmth of the towels, the clean smell of the soap and the repeated, simple movements of her hands, and she found the rhythm unexpectedly soothing. She did not fold any faster than before, but she finished feeling that something had been completed instead of merely escaped.

Hana decided to make soup from start to finish at the pace of a person with nothing else to do, which, for the first time in her life, was true. She listened to the steady tap of the knife on the board, smelled the onion softening in the pot and watched the steam curl upward in the light from the window. It was not the best soup she had ever made, but it was certainly the one she had been most present for.

One wet afternoon Samir invited the little group to visit his workshop at the end of the street, which he had not opened to anyone since he retired. It smelled of sawdust, linseed oil and old coffee, and every tool hung in its own outline on the wall, as exact and unhurried as the words of a dictionary. Mrs Okoro said that it was the tidiest room she had ever seen, and Samir said that this was only because he had had forty years to practise.

Samir handed Teo a small, rough wooden box and a block wrapped in sandpaper, and showed him how to rub gently along the grain and never against it. Teo worked in long, even strokes, breathing out with each one in the rhythm that the walks had taught him, and a whole hour passed without a single glance at his phone. When he ran his thumb over the finished lid and felt it perfectly smooth, he smiled like a much younger boy.

In the yard behind the workshop Hana raked the fallen leaves into a great rustling heap, drawing the rake towards her in long strokes and letting her breath move with them. The tool made a soft and steady whisper against the ground, and the red and gold of the leaves seemed brighter to her than any autumn she could remember. Mei, who had come for the weekend, took a running jump into the heap and scattered about an hour's work in a second.

One busy morning, with guests expected and her mind already at the table, Hana forgot everything she had learned and chopped the carrots at her old postwoman's speed. The knife slipped and cut her finger, not seriously, but enough to bleed on the board and to make her sit down with a plaster and a thumping heart. She did not scold herself, since that would have been a second cut, but she did notice that the lesson had arrived with great clarity.

Hana had delivered many thousands of postcards in her working life, but she had not written one herself for a very long time, and she sat down to write to Mei with a pleasant sense of occasion. She formed each letter slowly, in her best handwriting, chose every word as if it were being weighed, and drew a small snail in the corner with a smile on its face. She posted it herself, and then waited at the postbox for a moment, feeling that she had joined the other side of her own profession.

Mrs Okoro invited Hana to her kitchen to learn how to make bread, and showed her how to push, fold and turn the dough in a steady rhythm that seemed to match the breath. Then, to Hana's amusement, there was nothing to do at all but wait for two hours while it rose, since yeast, as she remarked, is exactly like wood and cannot be rushed. Biscuit lay under the table and watched them with the patience of a creature who knew that something good would come out of the oven.

For one whole day Hana tried to do only one thing at a time, without the radio, the telephone or three jobs half-begun, and then she wrote down the result in her notebook. She had not, she noted honestly, got more done than usual, but she felt far less scattered, and she remembered reading that many people make more mistakes and work more slowly when they keep switching between tasks. She underlined the word many, because she did not wish to claim more than the evidence allowed.

In November came the anniversary of the death of her husband Laszlo, four years before, and the sky that morning was as grey and low as a lid. Hana woke feeling as heavy as a wet coat, and she stood for a long time at the window with his photograph in her hands, looking at his crooked smile. She had not told anyone what day it was, and she was not sure that she wanted to.

Hana went out to the river, and instead of pushing the sadness away as she had done for four years, she allowed it to walk beside her like another person on the Path. Samir appeared at the willows, read her face in a moment and fell into step with her without a word, and he made no attempt whatever to cheer her up or to mend what could not be mended. It was, she thought, quite simply the best thing that anyone could possibly have done for her that day.

Hana noticed the tightness in her chest and the lump at the base of her throat, and she did not try to argue them away or pretend that they were not there. She simply breathed gently, with one hand on her ribs, and let the sadness rise and ebb like a tide on a long, grey beach, without promising herself that it would end by lunchtime. It did not end, of course, but it moved, and that, she found, was really something.

Later, on the Bench, Samir said quietly that he had sat in that same place on many mornings with sadness of his own, and that he had never found a way to make it disappear. Grief, he said, is not a problem to be solved, but something that love leaves behind, and the most that a person can do is to carry it with a little more kindness. Hana nodded, unable to speak, and let the last of the willow leaves fall quietly around them as they sat.

That evening Hana told Judit how heavy the day had been, which she would never have done a year earlier, and her daughter listened without hurrying her. As a nurse, Judit gently reminded her that walking is no replacement for help, and they agreed that if the sadness lasted for weeks or grew too heavy, Hana would speak to her doctor. It was a good agreement, and Hana was grateful to have a daughter who knew when to be practical.

A cyclist swept round the corner so close to Hana that his handlebar brushed her sleeve, and a wave of hot anger surged up in her. Instead of shouting after him she stood still, took one long breath and allowed the out-breath to carry some of the heat away, and by the time she had finished, the cyclist was out of sight. She was still annoyed, as anyone would be, but she was no longer ruled by the annoyance, and that felt like a small victory.

One night Hana woke at three in the morning and began, as one does at that hour, to worry about money, the roof, her pension and a thousand imaginary disasters. She counted her out-breaths until the worry slowed and shrank to a more reasonable size, and when sleep still refused to return she got up, made a cup of tea and sat by the window. Breathing, she noted, is not a switch that turns off a restless mind, but it helps a little, and there was no shame in tea.

On the Bench Samir showed Hana how to move her attention slowly through her body from her feet to the crown of her head, noticing each part without trying to change it. She discovered that she held worry in her belly, anger in her jaw and fear in her hands, which were clenched in her lap like two small fists. It was not a cure, he said, but a way of finding out what was going on before it came out as a shout.

Mrs Okoro announced one wet morning that feelings are like weather, and Samir laughed and said that the image was very old but that it had lasted because it was true. We cannot choose what weather arrives, he said, nor make it leave by shouting at it, but we can decide whether to carry an umbrella, and that is nearly all that anyone can do. Teo, who was holding the only umbrella, handed it round to the group with a perfectly straight face.

Mrs Okoro mentioned that she often felt short of breath on the stairs, and she wondered aloud whether the walking and breathing might cure it. Samir told her kindly but firmly that breathing exercises are not a treatment for any illness, that trouble with breathing should always be looked at by a doctor and that the sooner she went, the better. She made an appointment that very afternoon, and the doctor, as it turned out, had something simple that could help.

When winter arrived, the walkers could see their breath rising before them in small clouds, which hung in the cold air for a moment and then vanished. Mei, who was wrapped in a scarf so thick that only her eyes were visible, breathed out as slowly as she could to make the longest cloud, and soon every member of the Snail Club was competing. The breath, Hana thought, had always been there, and it took the frost to make it visible.

One morning a thick white fog lay on the river, and the Bridge vanished completely, so that the walkers seemed to move through a room whose walls were made of cloud. The world shrank to a few metres around them, and sounds that were usually drowned by sight, the drip of the willows, the soft slap of the water, the far-off bark of a dog, became strangely clear. Nobody wished to hurry, and in that thick white silence nobody could have done so safely even if they had tried.

On a frosty morning the grass crunched under their boots like breakfast cereal, and every leaf along the Path was edged with a fur of glittering ice. The ground was treacherously slippery, and Samir remarked, with some satisfaction, that slow and careful steps were by far the safest kind, and that for once the world agreed with him. Hana walked heel to toe with her arms a little out, like a tightrope walker, and loved every step.

The first snow fell overnight, and in the morning the whole Path was white and hushed, as though the world had been wrapped in cotton wool. When Hana looked back along the bank she saw a line of footprints following them like a patient shadow, and she remembered the boot print in the mud that Samir had once shown her. It was the same lesson, she thought, only written larger and in softer handwriting, and it was far easier to read.

In the hardest cold Samir advised the group to wrap a scarf loosely over the nose and mouth, so that the air was warmed a little on its way in, and to dress in thin layers. He added, with a seriousness that Hana respected, that anyone with trouble in the chest or heart should ask a doctor before walking in severe cold, and that no morning was worth a risk. They all nodded gravely, and Teo, who always overdid things, wrapped his scarf twice round his neck for good measure.

In January Hana caught a heavy cold, and for a week she lay in bed with a blocked nose, an aching head and a mountain of tissues. She breathed through her mouth, which she did not enjoy, and she made no attempt to practise anything, since Samir had taught her that nothing in the practice should be forced when the body was struggling. For the first time in her life she allowed herself to be ill without feeling that she was failing a test.

While Hana was ill, the others went on walking without her, and each in their own way found a means of letting her know. Judit brought soup between shifts, Mrs Okoro sent a warm loaf by Mei, and Teo left on the doorstep a tiny wooden snail that he had carved in Samir's workshop, with a note saying get well slowly. Hana set it on her windowsill beside the photograph, and she found that she was smiling at both.

When Hana was finally well enough to return to the Path, her legs felt weak and wobbly, as though they belonged to someone half her age and twice her anxiety. She walked only half the usual distance, resting twice, and for the first time she understood that a slow pace is not only a way of seeing but also a kindness to a tired body. Nobody mentioned the shortened walk, and Samir only said that he was glad to see her.

On the Bench Hana sat for a long time with her shoes off and her feet on the cold boards, getting her breath back and feeling slightly embarrassed. Samir said that rest is not the opposite of the practice but a part of it, that a tired body has its own wisdom, and that slow walking should never be pushed any more than the breath should be forced. Hana found that she was relieved to be told, since she had half suspected that she was supposed to be heroic.

On the iciest mornings of the winter the Path was too dangerous to walk, so Samir opened his workshop and the Snail Club walked up and down between the benches instead. It was a very short route, scarcely twelve paces long, but they discovered that the attention they brought to it was exactly the same, and that nothing in the practice depended on the scenery. Afterwards they drank hot tea beside the stove, and Biscuit slept on a pile of wood shavings with a sigh of deep contentment.

All through the winter the two sisters spoke every Sunday evening, and week by week the awkward silences grew shorter and the stories longer, until they had almost forgotten how bad it had been. In February Edith said, in an offhand voice that did not deceive anyone, that she would quite like to come and stay for a weekend, if there were room. Hana, standing at the kitchen table, took a breath before she answered, and found that her voice was perfectly steady.

Hana made up the bed in the spare room with unusual care, smoothing the sheet, plumping the pillows and putting a small jar of snowdrops beside the lamp. She noticed that she was nervous, and she noticed the old urge to scrub something spotless, and then she took her breath at the front door and let the urge go by. The cupboards, for once, were left in peace, and she felt that they were grateful.

The train was twenty minutes late, and Hana, who in her working years would have paced the whole length of the platform and cursed the railway, simply stood and breathed and felt her feet on the cold concrete. When Edith finally stepped down from the carriage, holding a small blue suitcase, she looked smaller and a little older than Hana remembered, and the sight of her went straight to Hana's heart. They embraced awkwardly at first, and then, after a moment, not awkwardly at all, which was a great relief to both.

Edith set off from the station at such a pace that Hana, who for months had been practising the opposite, had to take a couple of quick steps to keep up with her. She began to laugh, because she recognised in her sister's brisk, hunched back the exact figure that she herself had been until the previous spring. Their mother, Hana remembered, had walked in just the same way, as if the pavement owed her money.

Over soup at the kitchen table the sisters talked for hours, about their childhood, their mother's habits, the neighbours and Edith's new job, until the conversation wandered, as it was bound to, into the quarrel itself. When an old hurt came back into the room, Hana felt the familiar heat rise, took one slow breath and listened instead of leaping in, and the heat passed without having done its usual damage. Edith noticed the pause, and she let her own shoulders come down a little, as if answering it.

Each sister said, at last, what she had needed in that terrible year, and each apologised for particular words that she had said and could not unsay. They both wept, and neither pretended that everything was now mended, since the flat was still sold and the past still the past, but something that had been wound very tight inside each of them became a little looser. Hana thought that this was a more honest ending than a perfect one would have been.

The next morning Edith joined the Snail Club at the willows, announcing in advance that she thought the entire idea sounded rather silly and that she would walk with them out of politeness. Hana did not argue, for she remembered perfectly well how she herself had arrived, and Samir merely handed Edith a tin cup of tea and said that politeness was an excellent beginning. By the first bend she had slowed down, although she would have denied it under oath.

At first Edith found the slow pace almost maddening, and she sighed so loudly and so often that Biscuit began to look concerned. Then she saw Gertie standing in the shallows, as still as a stone, and she stopped for a full minute and noticed, with a kind of dismay, how quick and shallow her own breathing was. She did not say that she was converted, but she said that she would think about it, which Hana knew was the first step.

On the Bench the sisters began to talk about their mother, who had walked so fast but hummed so softly, a little tuneless melody that neither of them could ever name. They tried to recall it, quarrelled amiably about the second line and then hummed it together, rather badly, beside the river, while Samir politely studied the water. It was the first time since the funeral that either had been able to think of her without a stab of pain.

On Sunday evening Edith took the train home, and there were no big speeches on either side, only a long hug, a wrapped slice of cake and a promise that they would meet again in the spring. Hana stayed on the platform until the lights of the train had disappeared round the bend, breathing slowly, feeling a sadness that had a warmth at its centre. She walked home at her new pace, and the town, in the lamplight, seemed unusually kind to her.

One late-winter morning Samir announced that he would be away for a month, staying with his daughter Leyla in a distant city, because she had just had a baby and needed help. He was visibly delighted, as grandfathers are, but he also looked a little worried about leaving the little group, like a man handing over a delicate piece of furniture. Nobody told him that there was no need to worry, because it would not have been true.

On the first morning without Samir the group gathered beneath the willows and stood about in a kind of polite uncertainty, like guests at a party whose host has gone out. Their own rule said that nobody should lead, and yet, by a process that nobody could afterwards describe, Hana discovered that she was standing a little in front of the others, and they were looking at her. She felt precisely as she had felt on her first morning in retirement, only with an audience.

Hana protested that she was no teacher and had been practising for scarcely a year, and that Samir had forty years more experience of everything. Mrs Okoro replied, with the practical air of a woman who had raised a family, that nobody had asked her to teach anything, only to walk at the front, which she had been doing well for months. Teo shrugged, in his usual manner, and said that it sounded perfectly fine to him, and the matter was settled.

The walk went smoothly, and in the pale morning light the river looked exactly as it had on every other day, as if it had never heard of leaders. Hana realised, with a slight shock, that the practice did not belong to Samir or to anyone else, but was something that all of them were rediscovering together. The Path, she decided, belonged to whoever walked it, and the practice, in the same way, to whoever tried it.

Mrs Okoro asked why slow breathing seems to calm people, and Hana, who would once have invented an answer to fill the silence, found that she simply did not know. She said so honestly, adding that scientists are still studying the matter and that the results differ, and she felt a pleasant lightness at having admitted it. She suspected that Samir would have approved, and that saying I do not know was an important part of being a guide.

A postcard arrived from Samir, bearing a photograph of a baby's tiny hand curled round a large, work-roughened finger, and Hana picked it up from the doormat with an old postwoman's expert fingers. On the back he had written only two words, walk slowly, in the careful square capitals of a man who had spent his life marking planks. She read it twice standing in the hall, and then she propped it against the clock, where she could see it.

Before an important school exam Teo came to the willows looking pale and nervous, with his bag over one shoulder and his fingers drumming against his leg. They walked together at an extra gentle pace, breathing in for four steps and out for six, and Hana told him honestly that it would not make the nerves vanish. She added that it might give him somewhere to put his attention, and that if the worry ever grew too large to carry, he should speak to his mother or his teacher, and Teo said that he knew.

Hana invited old Mr Varga to join the walks, and one grey morning he appeared at the willows in his best brown coat, leaning heavily on a stick and looking as though he expected to be sent home. He was the slowest walker of them all, and without a word being spoken the whole group slowed to match him, so that the Snail Club discovered that there is a speed slower than slow. Mr Varga, who had not been part of anything for years, smiled the whole way.

In late February the snowdrops pushed up through the cold ground beside the Path, small and white and undefeated, and the willows showed the first yellow-green hints of their buds. Hana felt the year coming round, like a clock whose hands had travelled all the way and were nearing the place where they began, and she realised that she had been walking slowly for almost a year. She stood and breathed in the cold, clean air and thought that it smelled faintly of beginnings.

Samir came back at the end of the month, a little thinner and entirely delighted, with a new photograph for every member of the Snail Club. He told them that a newborn baby breathes much faster than an adult, often thirty to sixty times a minute, which had amazed him, and that he was sorry to find them so well able to manage without him. Hana replied, without a trace of hesitation, that he was very much needed, because nobody else could carry the flask.

In March the librarian from the town library invited the Snail Club to lead a slow walk across the Bridge on a Sunday in April, as part of the town's spring fair. Hana protested that they were not experts, and the librarian replied, with a twinkle, that this was precisely why she had asked, since the town had enough experts and not nearly enough people who simply walked. Hana said that she would have to consult the others, and she consulted them on the way home.

Everyone helped with the preparations, each in a different and characteristic way, and the whole street seemed to hum with it. Teo designed a poster in careful lettering, Mei drew a procession of snails across the bottom of it, Mrs Okoro promised thirty small loaves and Mr Varga, once a gardener, mended a broken bench. Hana wrote the notices by hand, which took a whole evening, and which she enjoyed from the first word to the last.

Hana grew more nervous as the day approached, and she asked Samir what on earth she should say to a crowd of strangers. He considered the question for a good while and then told her to say a little less than she wanted to, and to trust the walking to say the rest. She wrote three sentences on a small card, walk slowly, breathe gently and never force it, and was astonished by how much of the year they held.

On Sunday morning, to Hana's complete astonishment, about sixty people gathered at the near end of the Bridge in the bright April sunshine. There were children and grandparents, three teenagers with their hoods up, a man in a business suit who looked as though he had come by mistake and a great many dogs, all apparently waiting for her. She looked for Samir, and found him at the back, smiling, and absolutely not coming to help.

Hana read out her three sentences from the little card, and the crowd was so quiet that she could hear the river under the Bridge. Then she added something of her own, which was that none of this was a cure for anything, and that anyone with trouble breathing or a long, heavy sadness should please speak to a doctor. There was a murmur of approval, and she felt, to her relief, that she had said exactly enough.

Sixty people walked across the old stone Bridge at a snail's pace, and for ten minutes the only sounds were the murmur of the river and the laughter of a toddler leading his father by the finger. Hana walked at the front with Mei, and she could hear, behind her, the soft, shuffling sound of the whole town slowing down. It was the nearest thing to a miracle that she had ever witnessed, and nobody had to believe in anything.

Afterwards a man in a tracksuit told Hana, quite politely, that he thought the whole thing was nonsense, because he walked fast every morning for his health and felt fine. Hana agreed cheerfully that fast walking is good for many people, that she had done plenty of it herself, and that there is no single right way to walk, only different ways of paying attention. The man looked a little disarmed, and then he asked, almost against his will, how one began.

Teo's mother found Hana in the crowd and thanked her with such warmth that Hana had to look at the river, saying that her son seemed calmer and kinder than he had been for years. Teo rolled his eyes in the traditional manner of sixteen-year-olds and muttered that he did not have to love everything about it, he simply came, and Hana understood that this was his highest praise. His mother squeezed his arm, and he pretended to be looking at a bird.

Afterwards there was hot tea and fresh bread under the willows, and a woman whom Hana had never met asked in a low voice how a person should begin. Hana looked at her for a moment and said that she could simply stand still, feel her feet on the ground for one minute and breathe in her ordinary way, and that this was already the whole practice. The woman said that it sounded too easy to be true, and Hana said that it was easy, and that this was the difficult part.

That evening Hana confessed to Samir that she had been terribly nervous all day, and he admitted, to her surprise, that he had stood at the back of the crowd with his heart pounding on her behalf. They sat on the Bench until dusk, watching the river turn from silver to pewter, and the warmth of the day slowly left the stones around them. It struck her that she had been neither fast nor slow that day, but only there.

A full year after her first morning of retirement, Hana woke at five, as she still did without the help of any alarm, and lay in the pale light listening to the dawn chorus outside her open window. The quiet that had once felt so hollow now seemed full of small, bright voices, a blackbird, a robin and somewhere a very ambitious wren. She smiled at the ceiling, and she was in no hurry whatever to get up.

Hana walked along the river path at a pace that was neither slow nor fast but simply hers, noticing the blossom on the hawthorn, the ripples round a post and the little ginger cat on the wall. When she reached the bend where Samir stood waiting, she did not overtake him, as she had done on the first morning, but stopped and fell into step beside him without even thinking about it. They both noticed what had happened, and neither of them said a single word about it, which was exactly right.

Samir remarked, in the mild tone that she had come to love, that the Path was never really for getting anywhere, and that it had taken him many years to understand this and no time at all to forget it. Hana laughed and said that after a whole year of walking it she felt as if she had arrived everywhere, one small step at a time. Samir said that it was an excellent summary and that she should write it down.

On the Bench Hana opened her notebook and began, with the care of a woman writing an address on a parcel, a short list of what a year had taught her. She wrote that one should feel the feet on the ground, let the steps and the breath move together, let the out-breath be long and gentle and never, under any circumstances, force anything. She read it over and thought that it looked smaller than the year had felt, and that perhaps this was how true things usually looked.

On the second page she recorded that the senses dwell always in the present, and that it helps to attend to one task at a time, and to regard a leaf as though it might be the last one. When the mind wanders, as it certainly will, she added, return without reproach, and do this as many times as it takes, which will be a great many. Beside the list she drew a small snail, since the list seemed incomplete without one.

On the last page Hana wrote that the real place to practise is not the river but the rest of one's life, with its doors, its telephones, its queues and above all the person in front of you. A walk beside water is a pleasure, she added, but the true test is whether the same attention can be brought to a difficult conversation or a long wait. She wrote the word kindly at the bottom and underlined it, and then put the notebook away.

In the afternoon Edith arrived for the spring visit that she had promised, carrying the same small blue suitcase, and she walked from the station a little more slowly than before, while insisting that this was entirely an accident. Hana linked arms with her and said nothing, since she remembered all too clearly how it felt to be told that one was changing. They went home by the river, and Edith stopped, twice, to look at things.

Hana walked hand in hand with Mei beneath the falling white blossom, and she was quietly honest with herself about the year. She still forgot, sometimes for days at a time, she still hurried when she was late, she still did not understand half of what she had read, and she still began again, every single time. Mei, who had no interest in such matters, was trying to catch a petal before it reached the ground.

Beside the Bridge, Gertie the heron stood in the shallows, as still as a stone and as patient as a monk, while the whole Snail Club gathered quietly on the bank. Then, with no warning, she lifted from the water on a slow, deep beat of her great grey wings and sailed off downstream, trailing her long legs behind her. Nobody spoke, and Mei counted her breaths aloud, in a whisper, until the bird was out of sight.

That is all there is to it: walk slowly, breathe without force, notice the world around you and arrive again and again at each step, for as long as it feels good to do so.
